The API time of the BFME2 and RotWK load screens drops by 25-45 % in every pair (the spread between pairs is smaller
than the gain); the time to play follows in four pairs of five (the fifth lost on I/O wait, not API time). BFME1's map
load is guest-bound and uses no D3DX image work: the same time within the spread (the `GetDesc` fast path removes
~150 ms of API time, lost in the noise). Runs not counted: one BFME2 pair and one BFME1 pair where the menu was too
slow under the server's load for the scenario's clicks to start the map (both sides), and a BFME1 variant that hit the
intermittent access violation in the game's heap code during the menu, which base `main` also shows (the race under
investigation in the green-thread scheduler; no D3DX image call there).

Re-measured after review (2026-10-14, code unchanged — only tests and this text —, Node `startbench` with a fresh
profile each side, base `ca01ae8` and this branch at the same time, launch order alternated, 1-minute load 17-25; "API"
is the API time of the load + loadscreen phases):

| Run (pair, first launched) | load + loadscreen | API time | FilterTexture / LoadSurfaceFromMemory | thread CPU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BFME2 bfme2-startup, base first | 21.8 -> 17.7 s | 5 237 -> 2 201 ms (-58 %) | 1 471 -> 393 / 2 097 -> 619 ms | 21.7 -> 17.6 s |
| BFME2, variant first | 22.3 -> 18.7 s | 5 593 -> 2 326 ms (-58 %) | 1 571 -> 450 / 2 301 -> 616 ms | 22.1 -> 18.6 s |
| RotWK rotwk-startup, base first | 21.1 -> 19.2 s | 3 193 -> 2 082 ms (-35 %) | 560 -> 618 / 1 174 -> 308 ms | 20.4 -> 18.7 s |
| RotWK, variant first | 17.7 -> 15.6 s | 2 838 -> 1 126 ms (-60 %) | 517 -> 126 / 1 058 -> 273 ms | 17.0 -> 15.0 s |
| RotWK, base first | 20.1 -> 18.2 s | 3 012 -> 1 305 ms (-57 %) | 543 -> 91 / 1 093 -> 302 ms | 19.5 -> 17.5 s |

Every pair gains in time to play (2-4 s) and API time; the gain is well beyond the spread between pairs. One outlier:
in the first RotWK pair the variant's `D3DXFilterTexture` took 618 ms for its 592 calls (91-126 ms in the two other
variant runs) — a stall of one run (the large DXT levels go to the helper pool, which waits for helpers on a loaded
server), not reproduced.

The 16-bit decode alone (`toRgba` of an R5G6B5 / A4R4G4B4 256 x 256 image, `d3dx-image-bench.mjs`) is the one operation
where the kernels barely help: it is a table lookup per texel in JavaScript already, and the kernel adds a copy in and
a copy out. A verification run on the loaded server (1-minute load 30-59, 9 runs) found it slower than the base (A/B
1.10-2.02 for R5G6B5, 1.07-1.39 for A4R4G4B4, +0.03-0.5 ms per image); re-run at load 17-22 with 15 runs it was faster
in each of 6 runs (A/B 0.62-0.86 and 0.60-0.89), and in-process against the same tree's JavaScript path
(`ORTHROS_DXT_WASM=0` toggled, 200 interleaved calls) 0.18-0.23 against 0.20-0.27 ms (R5G6B5, one run of three slower
by 6 %) and 0.10 against 0.14-0.15 ms (A4R4G4B4). Within the noise of a loaded server, so kept: the same kernel feeds
the in-memory mip chains of 16-bit sources (A1R5G5B5 chain 0.35 -> 0.12 ms), and no game run shows a 16-bit decode on
its own among the costly calls.

## Measuring within a session

Harness inputs (tools/headless.mjs): `dbg:ORTHROS_API_OPT_OFF=1` switches all of the above off (`=` back on) except
the D3DX image work: of that section, `ORTHROS_API_OPT_OFF` and `ORTHROS_D3DX_FAST_OFF` cover only the surface `GetDesc`
fast path, `dbg:ORTHROS_DXT_WASM=0` puts the image kernels (and the helpers' encoder) back on JavaScript, and the GUID
string cache, the header-only TGA / BMP information, DDS files read in place and the lighter `LockRect` have no switch;
`dbg:ORTHROS_GL_NOCACHE=1` only the backend's caches; `dbg:ORTHROS_D3DX_FAST_OFF=1` only the JIT fast paths;
`dbg:ORTHROS_FX_BIND_OFF=1` only the effect binding above (raw words, versions, sampler shortcut, resolved methods);
`dbg:ORTHROS_FX_DEFER_OFF=1` only the queued `SetTechnique` / `Begin` / `End` (also off with the D3DX fast paths).
Scenarios `tools/scenarios/{bfme2,rotwk}-apiopt-{ab,ba}.txt` alternate 20 s phases on / off in play (both orders),
`{bfme2,rotwk}-fxbind-ab.txt` the same for the effect binding, `{bfme2,rotwk}-fxdefer-{ab,ba}.txt` for the queued
technique calls (both orders). Tools: `tools/draw-bench.mjs` (device + backend per draw over a counting GL), `tools/setter-bench.mjs` (the
queued setters), `tools/effect-bind-bench.mjs` (effect setters and binds, `--base <tree>` against another checkout),
`tools/effect-object-bench.mjs` (the effect calls of an engine drawing objects — technique, ~15 parameters, Begin,
BeginPass, commits, End — over 6 effects with array-selected shaders, preshaders and expression states; `--jit`: as
guest code through the JIT and the deferred queue; `--base <tree>`; best read as instructions under `perf stat -e
instructions:u`, insensitive to the server's load). Test of the effect binding: `d3dx9-effect-bind.test.js` (random
sessions against the reference path, registers bit for bit).
`dbg:ORTHROS_DRAW_OPT_OFF=1` handles the draws at their call again and switches the lights / material / FVF filter off
(`=`: back on, the filter once the queue has run): `Jit.setDrawOpt`. (The fix of the clobbered spec, section 1, has no
switch.)

## Draw submission per draw (2026-10-06)

**Where it went.** BFME1's 3D main menu in Node (`tools/framebench.mjs --gfx recorder`, the render worker's recording
with its commands dropped; 830-890 draws per frame), V8 profile of 300 frames, per frame: the JavaScript API calls 5.0
ms, of which `IDirect3DVertexBuffer9::Unlock` 1.1 ms (all of it the copy of the written ranges into the command ring,
2.5-2.7 MB per frame), `DrawIndexedPrimitive` 0.7 ms (the recorder's `flush` 0.6), the queued calls 1.3 ms (7 000-8 000 per
frame: `LightEnable` 2 100, `SetLight` 2 100, `SetTransform` 750, `SetTextureStageState` 630, `SetRenderState` 420,
`SetIndices` 350...), the dispatcher's own work 0.6 ms (2 700 calls handled in JavaScript per frame: 840 draws, 165 + 145
vertex / index buffer Lock / Unlock pairs, heap calls). Counted per queued method, the calls that changed the device:
`SetLight` 0 of 2 078, `LightEnable` 33 of 2 095, `SetSamplerState` / `SetTextureStageState` / `SetIndices` hundreds that
the filter should have dropped — the clobbered spec of section 1.

**Changes** (section 1): the spec kept (the filter stays on after a queued structure), lights / material / FVF in the
filter, draws queued.

**Measured.**
- Deterministic in-session A/B (Node, `startbench --virtual`: the same guest work in both runs; BFME1 3D main menu, 40 s
  of virtual time in 8 phases of 5 s, `dbg:ORTHROS_DRAW_OPT_OFF` alternated, run A starting on, run B off, both at
  once, the render worker's recording as backend): `api` on − off = −2.63 ms per frame (every phase lower: −1.35 to
  −4.02; api off 6.8-12.9 ms per frame in this slow virtual run); the emulator thread's CPU −0.96 ms per frame with a
  spread of ±5 ms per phase between the runs (warm-up, V8 tiering), host instructions of the thread −6.8 M per frame
  (spread ±15 M): within the noise of whole-thread measures.
- Base against this branch (same deterministic run, both at once, everything included): BFME1 menu phase of
  `bfme-phases.txt` (1 046 frames, 28.13 G guest instructions in both) `api` 6.88 → 5.92 ms per frame, thread CPU 62.6 →
  60.2 ms per frame; Node `framebench` pairs before the queued draws (filter only): `api` 4.38 → 3.97 and 3.66 → 3.45 ms per
  frame, wall per frame −1.4 / +0.7 ms (noise).

**Measured again with every change (2026-10-14; base = the tree before them, both runs at once, launch order alternated,
per frame base → branch).**
- Node, virtual clock (the same guest work in both runs, identical guest instruction counts): BFME1 3D menu `api` 4.34 →
  3.25 ms (two pairs, identical), emulator thread CPU 65.6-67.5 → 62.7-63.7; BFME1 menu `api` 3.58-3.65 → 3.05-3.11, thread
  CPU 37.6-38.2 → 36.3-36.4; BFME2 (`bfme2-startup.txt`, one pair) menu `api` 4.28 → 3.97, play 5.03 → 4.87 (thread CPU
  16.75 → 16.83: within the noise).
- Node, real clock: BFME1 play `api` 2.67 → 2.38 and 3.59 → 3.25 (fps 33.9 → 34.3, 30.4 → 30.8); Vice City drive `api`
  1.96 → 1.45 and 2.23 → 1.72, thread CPU 14.4 → 12.6 and 16.9 → 14.9. BFME2 play: `api` 5.82 → 6.60 and 6.76 → 8.12, but
  not the same work: in both real-clock pairs the branch's runs drew more per frame (46 effect `Begin` / `SetTechnique` per
  frame against 33, +6 % guest instructions), while in the virtual-clock pair (identical work) both run 33 — the game
  renders more when it has the time; per-frame figures do not compare there.
- Browser (`--gl-discard`, three BFME1 pairs, `bfme-phases.txt` with a 3D-menu phase; one pair on a machine at load
  30-40): 3D menu `api` 12.1 → 10.4, 5.7 → 4.4, 5.3 → 4.1 ms, fps 7.7 → 7.8, 18.0 → 18.1, 18.7 → 19.5; menu `api` 4.4 →
  4.1, 4.0 → 3.5, 4.0 → 3.3, fps 22.6 → 22.6, 24.2 → 24.5, 25.1 → 26.1; play `api` 5.9 → 4.9, 2.9 → 2.5, 3.5 → 3.0, fps
  23.8 → 24.7 (loaded), 38.3 → 38.3 twice (the frame pacing's cap); map load (loadscreen) 75.2 → 69.6, 61.9 → 61.6, 62.1
  → 62.1 s. BFME2 (two pairs, `bfme2-startup.txt`): menu `api` 5.2 → 4.3 and 5.2 → 4.6, play 30.2 / 30.1 fps in all four
  runs (`api` 4.7 → 5.0 and 4.9 → 6.0: the same "more drawn" effect as in Node).
- Fidelity: `?glworker=compare-worker` on the branch, BFME1 menu to play (35 frames compared, 0 differing) and Vice City
  drive (220-1 460 frames compared, 0 differing); the randomized suites (`jit-defer-filter*.test.js`) against executing
  every call.

**Measured, not done.** Of the 2.5 MB per frame copied into the ring at `Unlock` in that menu, a whole-buffer lock of a
dynamic vertex buffer without flags (1 per frame, 0.5-0.63 MB) never changes a byte, and the `NOOVERWRITE` / `DISCARD`
ranges change 30-50 % of their bytes but 70-85 % of their 256-byte blocks (a shadow copy compared at each `Unlock`). Sending
only the changed ranges would read twice the bytes it saves writing (the comparison against the shadow, then the shadow
updated); in JavaScript the comparison is slower than the copy (~1-2 GB/s against 5-6 GB/s for a typed-array copy into
shared memory, this machine). Only the unchanged whole-buffer lock would gain, ~0.1-0.2 ms per frame: not done.

## Win32 heap (src/win32/heap.js)

`HeapAlloc` was BFME1's costliest API call outside play. In Node (`startbench`, the runs below): 7-16 µs per call in
the menu (100-320 calls per frame), 25-150 µs in the seconds after the skirmish click (`load`: 11-65 ms per frame),
9-57 µs in the map load (`loadscreen`: 4-30 ms per frame); an earlier V8 profile gave `Heap.chunkOf` 10 % of the load
phase.
Counted (instrumented run): the game's own heap (`HeapCreate`, then `HeapAlloc` with `HEAP_ZERO_MEMORY`, 1 MB growth)
holds ~730 chunks in the menu and ~960 after the map load (~200 growths in the 10 s after the click), and `chunkOf`
scanned them one by one (~640 comparisons per call on average) — for every free block an allocation visits
(`freeBlockOk`: 1-4.6 per allocation on average, up to ~620 when a power-of-two class holds many smaller blocks), for
every `HeapFree` and `HeapSize`.

- **Chunk lookup in O(1)**: past 8 chunks, a heap keeps a map of the 64 KB granules of the 32-bit space (a `Uint16Array`
  of 65 536 entries, 128 KiB, only for heaps that large) giving the index + 1 of the chunk covering each granule. Chunks
  come from `VMem` 64 KB aligned and sized, so a granule belongs to one chunk at most; one shared by two chunks all the
  same (`SHARED`) is looked up by the linear scan, as are heaps of fewer chunks. `chunkOf` returns the chunk object the
  scan returns, for any number.
- **The allocation walk** checks each free block inline (`freeBlockOk`'s conditions, in the same order) with aligned
  `Uint32Array` reads instead of a method call and `DataView` reads per word. The walk, its order and its robustness
  checks are unchanged: the same block comes back for every request (which block a game gets back decides its reuse
  patterns, docs/thread-scheduling.md), the same lists are cut (`brokenLists`), the same links ignored (`plausible`).
- **`HEAP_ZERO_MEMORY`** (`zeroFill`): with the lookup fixed, zeroing was 55-85 % of `HeapAlloc`'s remaining time (the game
  zeroes every block: 13-100 MB per 10 s in the menu, ~40 MB per 10 s in the map load). On a shared guest memory (the
  browser with the background translator or the render worker, `startbench --bg`) a typed array's `fill` stores one
  element at a time: through the byte view 2.4 GB/s, through `Uint32Array` 5.3, `Float64Array` 6.6 (8.0-8.4 for all three
  on an unshared buffer); a 256-byte fill 0.197 against 0.056 µs. An 8-aligned range inside the memory is now filled as
  doubles (+0: eight zero bytes), anything else as before — the same bytes. (`GuestMemory.fill` itself, used by many other
  callers, still fills bytes: the same change there is left to a measurement of its own.)
- **Looping free lists**: the randomized test below found programs whose writes into freed blocks turn a free list into
  a loop of valid free blocks too small for the request — the walk never ended (the emulator hung). Brent's cycle
  detection (one comparison per step: a mark moved to the current block after 1, 2, 4... steps) finds the loop, and
  `cutLoop` ends the list at the last block of the loop (each block stays in the list once; `stats.loopedLists`). A
  walk that ends is not affected: nothing is written during a walk, so meeting a visited block again means it would
  repeat forever.

Tests: `heap-lookup.test.js` — `chunkOf` against the linear scan for boundary and random addresses (interleaved heaps,
granules shared by unaligned chunks, after `destroy`), and a differential run of random programs (allocations zeroed or
not, frees, reallocations in place or moved, zeroed or not, double frees, frees of non-blocks, the program's data in its
blocks, writes into freed blocks — links into the other heap, into nothing, unaligned, fake free blocks inside freed
blocks and against the chunk's end sentinel, sizes — and past the end of live blocks) on this heap and on the linear-scan
heap it replaced (old walk, old reallocation, byte fills), each in its own guest memory: same results, same contents read
back from every block handed out, same chunks, same bytes in every chunk, same list heads and counters. Each of 14 single
mutations of the new code (a check dropped or loosened, an off-by-one in the map or in a zeroed range) makes it fail.
`heap-corruption.test.js`: a two-block loop and a self-linked block behind another are cut, their blocks still found (2
more mutations of `cutLoop`).

**Measured (2026-10-06).** Microbenchmark (a heap grown to 900 chunks, alloc / free of mixed sizes, half zeroed;
concurrent pairs, two each): 15.3-15.4 → 0.72-0.79 µs per operation on an unshared memory, 18.3-18.5 → 0.93-1.03 µs on a
shared one; a heap of 22 chunks (small blocks, no zeroing, shared): 0.17-0.19 → 0.12-0.13 µs.

BFME1 in Node (`startbench --bg`, `tools/scenarios/bfme-phases.txt`; base and branch at the same time, launch order
alternated). The server's load average was 23-65 during these runs (other projects): in two pairs neither run reached
the skirmish (clicks timed in wall-clock seconds landing before the menus were ready), so pairs 4-8 used a copy of the
scenario with the menu's step times doubled (menu phase 270 s). Final code (pairs 7 and 8, launched branch first / base
first):

| phase | measure | pair 7 base → branch | pair 8 base → branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| menu (270 s) | `HeapAlloc` µs per call | 9.4 → 1.4 | 9.0 → 1.6 |
| | `HeapFree` µs per call | 2.9 → 1.1 | 3.2 → 1.1 |
| | `api` ms per frame | 3.37 → 2.59 | 3.30 → 2.78 |
| | frames | 6262 → 6404 | 6376 → 6492 |
| load (4-6 s after the click) | `HeapAlloc` µs per call (ms per frame) | 50.0 → 3.4 (23.5 → 1.7) | 77.0 → 2.8 (33.3 → 1.3) |
| loadscreen (map load) | duration | 60.3 → 60.8 s | 66.5 → 62.8 s |
| | `HeapAlloc` µs per call (ms per frame) | 11.3 → 2.0 (6.1 → 1.0) | 8.6 → 2.4 (4.2 → 1.1) |
| | `api` ms per frame | 16.4 → 10.8 | 16.1 → 10.4 |
| play (160 s) | `HeapAlloc` µs per call | 3.6 → 1.7 | 2.7 → 1.1 |

The chunk lookup alone (without the zero fill; pair 2 on the original scenario, pairs 4 and 5 on the slower one, plus
two pairs that only completed the menu): menu `HeapAlloc` 7.2-16.4 → 2.5-6.8 µs, `api` -0.6 to -2.3 ms per frame;
load 27-150 → 4.0-10.7 µs; loadscreen 9.6-56.7 → 5.3-8.6 µs (4.3-30.4 → 2.7-4.5 ms per frame). Across all seven pairs
whose menu phase completed, the branch drew more menu frames in every pair (+0.4 to +2.5 %: the menu is CPU-bound and
`api` is 8-9 % of its frame). The map load's duration did not move beyond its spread (differences +0.6, -2.5, -1.5,
+0.5, -3.7 s on loads of 54-73 s): the time saved in `HeapAlloc` there is 0.1-2 s per load. In a third final pair the
branch's run ended right after the skirmish-setup click: the game exited by itself (no Orthros crash report), as in
the known BFME1 race at that click, where the game's crash handler ends the process (docs/thread-scheduling.md, "The
BFME1 investigation": a few percent of runs, more under load; the load average was 44 then); that pair is not counted.

Browser (headless Chromium, `--gl-discard`, `bfme-phases.txt`, one pair at the same time, branch launched first; final
code), base → branch: boot to the menu (64 s) `HeapAlloc` 7.5 → 2.7 µs per call (1455 → 520 ms in total), `HeapFree`
2.5 → 1.4 µs; menu (134 s) `HeapAlloc` 4.8 → 1.9 µs (1632 → 642 ms), `HeapFree` 2.8 → 1.5 µs (1013 → 549 ms), `api`
5.4 → 4.8 ms per frame, 18.9 → 19.1 fps; load (5.5 s) `HeapAlloc` 45 → 4.9 µs (21.7 → 2.3 ms per frame), `api` 59 →
34 ms per frame; map load 66.2 s in both (its end is polled once a second), `HeapAlloc` 8.1 → 2.1 µs (323 → 79 ms);
play 31.8 → 32.0 fps, `api` 4.0 → 3.8 ms per frame (`HeapFree` 1641 ms, 8.3 µs per call, before; below the 12
costliest calls, under 754 ms, after). A single pair: the per-call figures are far outside any noise, the frame rates are not.

Not done: after a growth, `alloc` walks the size classes again although the first pass found nothing. Taking the new
chunk's block directly would return the same block in every case: the first pass only cut lists (broken or looping
ones, the rest of every list it walked holds blocks too small), and `grow` links the new block at the head of its class,
which is at least `classIndex(size)`, so the second pass reaches it after classes that still hold nothing large enough.
The lists could differ only in a forged corner case: `link` writes the back link of the old head of the new block's
class, and when the program built a fake free block whose header is that word, the second walk cuts the list holding
it. Growth happens once per new chunk (1 MB or more), so the saved walk is not measurable; left as it is.

The crash / hang report of `vm.js` lists every heap with overwritten boundary tags, broken free lists or looping free
lists (`stats.badTags`, `brokenLists`, `loopedLists`).

## Volume textures (2026-10-22)

Found by the survey of the Windows games (Node `startbench --bench`, COM failure reports): RotWK 2.01 creates a volume
texture (`D3DXCreateVolumeTexture`), takes its level 0 (`IDirect3DVolumeTexture9::GetVolumeLevel`), reads its
description, loads a DDS file into it (`D3DXLoadVolumeFromFileInMemory`) and builds its mips (`D3DXFilterTexture`).
`GetVolumeLevel` answered `E_NOTIMPL` (the game skipped the load: the texture stayed zero), the D3DX volume loads did
nothing, `D3DXFilterTexture` left a volume's mips empty, and a level written after the texture's first use was never
uploaded again (in-thread nor in the render worker). Now (d3d8.js `Volume`, shared by Direct3D 8 and 9):

- A volume texture's levels are `Volume` objects (IDirect3DVolume8 / 9: GetDevice, private data, GetContainer,
  GetDesc, LockBox, UnlockBox), one COM object per level, the same at each `GetVolumeLevel`, alive while the texture
  lives (as a texture's surface levels). `LockBox` with a box returns the pointer at its corner (front slice, top row,
  left column; 4 x 4 blocks for DXT), with the level's row and slice pitches.
- An unlock, a D3DX load or `UpdateTexture` (now between volume textures too) marks the level dirty: the backend
  uploads it again at the texture's next use. With the render worker, `VOL_MEM` carries a new generation (as
  `SURF_DIRTY`), so a later write to the texture waits for the commands that still read its old contents until the
  render worker acknowledges the upload (without it, a write made before the upload was replayed reached the GPU: the
  randomized replay tests, which lock volume levels, caught it).
- `D3DXLoadVolumeFromFileInMemory` (the file's first level, as is when the formats and sizes agree) and
  `D3DXLoadVolumeFromMemory` load a source box into a destination box of the level: converted through RGBA8, resized
  to the box (2 x 2 x 2 means or point), encoded slice by slice and written at the box's place (DXT: boxes on 4 x 4
  blocks). RotWK 2.01 loads 2D images into single slices of a 32 x 32 x 32 volume (box 0,0,32,32,z,z+1). `D3DXFilterTexture`
  of a volume texture computes each level from the one above, as RGBA8, each texel the mean of the 2 x 2 x 2 source box
  (fewer along an axis already at 1).

Tests: `tests/d3d-volume.test.js` (Direct3D 8 and 9 levels, descriptions, boxes, the D3DX loads — a slice box among kept slices — and
the mips against a direct computation, UpdateTexture; a destination box ignored fails one; a mutation restoring `E_NOTIMPL` fails 5 of 6, the box offset or the volume mips one
each), the render-worker replay tests (a mirror that does not mark the level dirty fails 4).

```

`docs/backups.md`:

```md
# Backups (restic)

Everything here that cannot be regenerated has one copy on this machine's disks. Since 2026-10-26 a restic repository
keeps its history: a file deleted or changed by mistake — a game's file, a manifest, an engine release, a player's
world, a local note — comes back as it was on any snapshot's date. `tools/backup.sh` is the only entry point (its
header lists the commands); the README's « Sauvegardes » section is the short version of this page.

## What a snapshot holds

| Source | What | Left out (and why) |
|---|---|---|
| `/srv/orthros` | `data/` (games, engines and their pinned sources, installers, Wine prefix, corpus, proofs), `backups/manual/`, `.git` (every commit and branch, the unpushed ones too), the local notes `CLAUDE.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `STATUS-history.md` (outside Git), the working tree and its uncommitted changes, `.charon-uploads/` | `build/`, `node_modules/`, `tests/generated/`, `.claude/worktrees/` (disposable or rebuilt); `backups/restic`, `backups/cache`, `backups/mnt`, `backups/restore-*`, the password file (the backups themselves) |
| `/var/lib/private/orthros2` | the server's accounts (players' cloud saves, Google sign-in configuration), learned data (orders, GL programs, snapshots), telemetry | `brcache/` and `covers/`: precompressed copies of the games' files and light covers, remade on demand |
| `/var/lib/private/orthros-goldsrc` | the GoldSrc dedicated servers' state | `*/game`: the linked game trees, rebuilt at each start |
| `/var/lib/orthros-openmw` | the OpenMW gateways' worlds, accounts, operator credentials, configuration | `*/gamedata`: the linked game trees, rebuilt at each start |
| `/etc` | `orthros-openmw.env` and the `orthros*` systemd units | |

Repository: `backups/restic/` (same NVMe disk as `data/`), password `backups/restic-password` (root, 0600), cache
`backups/cache/`. `backups/` is mode 0700 and ignored by Git (`/backups`, no trailing slash: a link of that name is
ignored too).

Restic stores content in deduplicated, compressed, encrypted chunks: a file present in every snapshot is stored once,
and a snapshot costs only the chunks that changed since the previous one. Game data is already compressed (BIG, BSA,
WAD archives), so the repository is about the size of what it holds. Measured on 2026-10-26 (restic 0.16.4, 4 cores):
the first snapshot read 114,691 files, 72.9 GiB (the hard-link copy of four games and duplicated installers counted
again), of which 29.9 GiB of distinct content, stored as 22.3 GiB, in 3 min 43 s; the next one, nothing changed but a
few state files, 5.6 s and 87 KiB.

## Schedule and retention

`orthros-backup.timer` runs `tools/backup.sh daily` every night at 04:40 (up to 15 min later; `Persistent=true`: a run
missed while the machine was off happens at boot): a snapshot tagged `daily`, then the retention policy and a prune.
Kept: every snapshot of the last 14 days, one per week for 8 weeks, one per month for 24 months, and always those
tagged `manual` (taken by hand) or `pre-restore` (taken automatically before an in-place restore). The service runs
niced (`Nice=19`, idle I/O, batch CPU) on 4 cores at most (`GOMAXPROCS=4`): this machine is shared.

`systemctl list-timers orthros-backup.timer` shows the next run; `journalctl -u orthros-backup` the last ones. A run
that finds a file unreadable (gone while read) still saves the snapshot (restic's exit 3) and says so in the journal.

## Using it (as root)

```sh
tools/backup.sh snapshot -m "before replacing bfme2's patch"   # before any hand change in data/ or the services' state
tools/backup.sh list                                          # the snapshots: id, date, tags (the note is a tag "note:…")
tools/backup.sh diff 1a2b3c4d latest                          # +/-/M per file between two snapshots
tools/backup.sh find manifest.json                            # every snapshot holding a file of that name, with its path
tools/backup.sh ls latest /srv/orthros/data/games/bfme1       # a folder's files in a snapshot
tools/backup.sh mount                                         # all snapshots as plain folders under backups/mnt/ (Ctrl-C)
```

Restoring:

- **A copy beside, nothing touched**: `tools/backup.sh restore <id|latest> <path> --to /tmp/orthros-scratch/restore`
  writes `<dir>/<absolute path>` (the scratch budget applies: a whole game can be 10 GB — prefer a single folder).
- **In place** ("revert"): `tools/backup.sh restore <id|latest> <path>` restores the snapshot's `<path>` into a stage
  under `backups/` (the same disk as `data/`), shows the changes (`rsync --itemize-changes`) and asks; then it takes a
  `pre-restore` snapshot of the current state, and makes `<path>` exactly as it was — files added since are removed
  (`rsync -aHAX --delete`). `--yes` skips the question (scripts, agents: only after reading the change list). The
  stage is removed at the end. A restore can therefore always be undone with the newest `pre-restore` snapshot.
- **A service's state** (e.g. an OpenMW world): stop its unit first (`systemctl stop orthros-openmw@<manifest>`),
  restore, start it again — a running service would overwrite or not see the restored files.
- **Everything after a disaster** (the folder deleted, the disk replaced): the repository lives on the same disk, so
  first recover `backups/` itself (see Limits); then
  `restic -r <repository> --password-file <file> restore latest --target /` puts every path back where it was.

Integrity: `tools/backup.sh check` (the repository's structure and a 1 % sample of the data, a minute or two);
`check --full` reads all of it. A run killed in the middle leaves a stale lock: `tools/backup.sh restic unlock`.

## Limits — what this does not protect against

- **The disk's loss**: the repository is on the same NVMe disk as `data/` (the owner's choice: inside `/srv/orthros`).
  It covers deletion and modification by mistake (a person, an agent, a bad merge as on 2026-10-02), not a dead disk
  or a lost VPS. A second copy is one command away when wanted: `restic copy` into a repository elsewhere — the
  machine's other disk (`/`, sda) or another machine (SFTP / S3) — run after `daily`.
- **The password**: without `backups/restic-password` no snapshot can be read. Keep a copy outside this machine
  (a password manager): `cat /srv/orthros/backups/restic-password`.
- **Databases copied live**: SQLite files (OpenMW's `accounts.db`, …) are read while their service runs, with their
  `-wal` / `-shm` files; SQLite recovers such a copy in practice, but a restore of one is best done with the service
  stopped and checked after its start.
- Data under `build/` and `/tmp/orthros-scratch` is never kept: nothing irreplaceable goes there (CLAUDE.md, Layout).

## History

Before 2026-10-26: four folders `data_games`, `data_engines`, `data_installers`, `data_wine` at the repository's root,
the OpenMW state under `build/openmw` (erased by `make clean`), and as the only protection a hard-link copy of four
games' folders (`data_installers/game-library-backup`, made after the 2026-10-02 incident: it survived a deletion of
`data_games` but shared every file with it — a file changed in place was changed in the "backup" too). It was removed
once the first snapshot was checked. DECISIONS.md D105.

```

`docs/browser-ports.md`:

```md
# Browser ports: games whose engine runs as browser code

Orthros runs games in the Win32 emulator and browser ports. All are declared by `data/games/<game>/manifest.json`, listed on the same home,
served by the same server (`src/host/server.js`, `orthros.service`) on the same origin. The version's `runtime` says
which kind it is:

- **`win32`** (the default): the unmodified Windows game in Orthros' own emulator (`src/cpu`, `src/loader`, `src/win32`,
  `src/gfx`, ...), written from scratch.
- **`goldsrc`**: a browser port. The game's original files run on a pinned third-party GoldSrc engine, Xash3D FWGS
  compiled to WebAssembly, with the game's client/server/menu modules compiled to WebAssembly too. Its page is
  `src/ports/goldsrc/`; it never loads the Win32 runtime, and the Win32 runtime never imports it.
- **`re3`**: a browser port. The game's original files run on a decompiled engine of the re3 family (reVC: Grand Theft
  Auto: Vice City's) compiled to WebAssembly, single player. Its page is `src/ports/re3/`; see "re3 ports" below.

Nothing in the code names a game: engine release, game directory, modules, maps and server ports come from the manifest.

OpenMW ports use `runtime: "openmw"`, their own page and a pinned OpenMW-Web engine. Their
multiplayer uses a native world gateway and simulation peers, proxied on the same origin.
See [OpenMW installation, pending data and validation](openmw.md). Several mods of the Vanilla+ profile are still
missing. A modded OpenMW game is a game of its own on the home (`modified`: its "Modified" tag), its version holding
only its mod stack: `requires` puts the original game's version's files beneath it, as for the ports below. Every game page — Windows games and ports — has the same frame (header, loading screen, account, saves):
[docs/game-frame.md](game-frame.md).

## Where things are

| Path | Content | In Git |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/host/goldsrc.js` | manifest checks, engine availability, multiplayer relay, linked game tree of the dedicated server | yes |
| `src/ports/goldsrc/` | the port's page (`play.html`, `play.js`, `storage.js`, `style.css`), `bsp-reads.js` (a map's load announced, below "Map loads announced") | yes |
| `src/host/re3.js`, `src/ports/re3/` | the re3 ports' manifest checks and engine availability; their page (`play.html`, `play.js`, `profile.js`, `ini.js`, `style.css`) | yes |
| `tools/re3/` | `lock.json` (the engine's pinned sources — Orthros' fork —, image, Emscripten ports and digests), `build.sh` (the engine from source), `patches/` (a build's own patches), `check.mjs` (browser check), `perf.mjs` (frame cost) | yes |
| `tools/goldsrc/` | `lock.json` (pinned upstream sources and artifacts, SHA-256), `install-engine.py`, `build-server.sh`, `build-modules.sh` with `patches/` (`hl-arsenal/`: the mod) and `cmake/` (game modules from source), `release-gamefiles.py` (a release's archives as loose game files), `bot-nav.mjs` (bots' navigation meshes), `server.mjs` (dedicated server), `orthros-goldsrc@.service`, `check.mjs` (browser check), `perf.mjs` (frame cost) | yes |
| `tools/port-perf.mjs` | the ports' shared frame measurement (below, "Measuring a port") | yes |
| `data/games/<game>/` | `manifest.json`, its cover (`coverFile`), `base/` (the original files), `versions/<version>/` | no |
| `data/engines/<release>/` | installed engines: `xash3d-web-1.2.2` (browser), `xash3d-web-1.2.2-cs16-15278ca-r2` and `…-arsenal-r12` (the same engine with Counter-Strike modules built from source), `xash3d-dedicated-e0ece3d` (native dedicated server), `revc-web-e312f97-r1` (reVC built from source) and `revc-web-e312f97-plus-r1` (with Orthros' additions) | no |
| `data/engines/src/` | upstream checkouts at their pinned commits: `xash3d-fwgs` (builds the dedicated server), `cs16-client` with its submodules (builds the Counter-Strike modules), `webxash3d-fwgs-cstrike` and `hlsdk-portable` (reference for later work), `reVC` (Orthros' fork) with its submodules, `emscripten-4.0.23-cache` (Emscripten's SDL2 and mpg123 ports, for builds without network) | no |

The engines stay out of Git like the games: the repository is public, the engine, wrapper and SDK-derived modules
carry their own licenses (notices below), and the browser game modules were recovered from a deployed build whose
sources no longer exist. `lock.json` and the install scripts reproduce them while their sources remain available;
treat `data/engines/` like `data/games/` (the only copy of the recovered modules).

### Measuring a port

`tools/re3/perf.mjs` and `tools/goldsrc/perf.mjs` share `tools/port-perf.mjs`: the browser's flags for a rendering
mode, a probe in the page before its scripts and its summary — the engine's work a browser frame (from its first
callback to the engine's request for the next), the gaps between frames shown, the WebGL calls a frame by kind with
the synchronous ones apart (getError, checkFramebufferStatus, readPixels, shader and program queries… — each one waits
for the GPU process; `--stacks getError` keeps their callers), the WebGL renderer (the checks print it too) — and a CPU
profile's summary (`--profile`: self time, the longest busy stretches). The page's telemetry and learning posts stay
off the server unless `--report`. Headless Chromium here always renders with SwiftShader: ANGLE's null backend
(`--use-angle=null`) is ignored — the renderer stays SwiftShader's with every flag combination (checked 2026-10-21), so
`--gl null` is refused. `--gl discard` (the default) keeps RASTERIZER_DISCARD on: every call validated and sent, the
vertex work done, no pixel drawn — the closest to the engine's own CPU cost a frame here, an upper bound
(SwiftShader's vertex threads still compete with the page: report the machine's load, several runs). `--gl swiftshader`
draws (the GPU's share on the CPU); `--gl gpu` adds no flag (a machine's own GPU).
The browser (`--channel`, `tools/openmw/perf.mjs` too) is Chromium itself in its new headless mode by default — as the
bench suite and the re3 check run it —; `--channel shell` takes Playwright's lighter headless shell, which measures
otherwise (2026-10-23): it composites the page differently (OpenMW's glide 47 frames a second there, 31 in Chromium and
in the suite), and once a page holds the pointer lock (reVC in the city, GoldSrc in a map) it sends that page about
40,000 synthetic mouse moves a second (zero movement; a trace: 308,583 `PostSynthesizeMouseMove` tasks in 6.5 s), its
browser thread and the page's compositor thread each a whole core — Chromium sends none, nor does any browser.

Where a port's frame goes outside its engine (2026-10-23, headless Chromium, SwiftShader, `--gl discard`): the WebGL
calls' execution in the GPU process. A frame waits for the previous one there; with a GPU process far behind, the time
shows as the browser's frames coming late (Chromium) or as GL calls blocking within the engine's work (the shell).
None of the ports makes a synchronous WebGL call a frame (reVC 0, OpenMW a getError every few seconds; the GPU timer's
`getQueryParameter` / `GPU_DISJOINT_EXT` are answered in the page, 2-3 µs, where a getError after a frame's draws
waits 42 ms here). Ablations: OpenMW standing at Seyda Neen (690 draws a frame, 6,300 calls) 17.7 frames a second,
the engine's work 22.5 ms; its draws made no-ops, 60 frames a second and 11.8 ms — SwiftShader's vertex work (on a
real GPU, 690 draws are a few ms of the GPU process). reVC: its `copyTexSubImage2D` (the colour filter's copy of the
screen, ~2 a frame) made a no-op, 30 frames a second instead of 16 (Chromium), 55 instead of 24 (shell) — a copy from
the `alpha: false` drawing buffer into an RGB texture, which ANGLE converts with a draw (a microbenchmark: two such
copies a frame cost 16.7 ms here, from an `alpha: true` buffer into RGBA nothing): a full-screen pass, a fraction of a
millisecond on a GPU. And reVC's 4x multisampled drawing buffer, which no setting asked for (below, "The engine, built
from source"): a real cost on every GPU, fixed. Canvas sizes: reVC draws at the canvas's CSS size whatever the
device pixel ratio; GoldSrc and OpenMW at device pixels (2560 × 1512 at a ratio of 2 — four times the pixels; OpenMW
caps the buffer at 4 MP and has its scene render scale per tier). The data indicator (`data-meter.js`, a 480 × 90
canvas drawn by a worker 10 times a second while shown) costs nothing measurable. It used to show "Loading…" over
smooth play (reVC driving at 24 frames a second): every read waiting for the network counted (`data-worker.js`
ctrl[6]), the engine's streaming asked ahead (`OrthrosFileReady`) and OpenMW's reads in the background (`readable`)
too. Now only the reads an engine waits for count (2026-10-23, `data-client.js` holdCheck): a synchronous one, and an
asynchronous one (JSPI `ensure`) when the engine has not gone on by the page's next task — an engine that suspends on
its read gives the page its turn having called nothing more, one that asked ahead reads, asks or shows its frame first
(`GameData.progress()`, the re3 page at each frame) —; a load of many short waits counts all along. Measured
(`tools/re3/perf.mjs` and `tools/openmw/perf.mjs` now report `meter`: the seconds it was shown, those the reads waited,
screenshots; `--net-after KB/s`: Chrome's link slowed from the measure on), rasterizer discarded, headless Chromium:
reVC driving (`--car GETTHEREFAST`, start at 3000 KB/s, 90 s driven at 300 KB/s) — shown 23.3 s at 28.5 frames a
second before (19.5 s of reads "waiting" while the engine stood 6.8 s), 0 s at 27.7 after; Morrowind's glide
(`--glide 1,0,600`, 60 s at 300 KB/s) — 22.8 s before, 6.8 s after (the page's synchronous reads held it 5.4 s);
Orthros Edition at 3000 KB/s: its start (the engine waits ~95 % of the time in reads of ~65 ms) and its free mode's
load shown, the menu and the walk not; the Win32 page (its own net status, `worker.js` netInfo, shown over the game only once its
frames stop 3 s) says it waits only at 0-15 frames a second (Vice City's loads), never over its menu at 60 or its game at 30.

On a player's machine (the owner's: a real GPU, Windows), the ports are measured by the **bench suite**
(`/?benchsuite=all`, docs/real-machine-bench.md "The bench suite"), every game in a row from one link, no Playwright:
the port's page opens in a frame of the Orthros page, `src/host/web/page-meter.js` measures its frames from outside it
(the same frame accounting, GPU timer and records as the Windows games'), `src/host/web/dom-input.js` gives it its
scenario's keys and clicks as DOM events, and its console (GoldSrc: `portSession.command`) or debug teleport (OpenMW:
`window.orthrosBenchHooks`, set by `src/ports/openmw/frame-meter.js` under `?benchrun=`) through hooks. The ports'
benches are in `tools/scenarios/bench/` (`revc-drive`, `morrowind-glide`, `halflife-c1a0`, `cs-bots`).

## Manifest

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1, "id": "half-life", "name": "Half-Life", "defaultVersion": "half-life-original-en",
  "defaults": { "runtime": "goldsrc", "coverFile": "cover.svg" },
  "versions": [{
    "id": "half-life-original-en", "dir": "original-en", "version": "Original · English", "languages": ["en"],
    "goldsrc": {
      "engine": "xash3d-web-1.2.2", "gameDir": "valve",
      "modules": { "client": "halflife/valve/cl_dlls/client_emscripten_wasm32.wasm",
                   "server": "halflife/valve/dlls/hl_emscripten_wasm32.wasm", "menu": "engine/libmenu.wasm" },
      "solo": { "map": "c0a0" },
      "multiplayer": { "server": "xash3d-dedicated-e0ece3d", "port": 28015, "map": "crossfire", "maxPlayers": 16 }
    }
  }]
}
```

The contract is in `game-manifest.schema.json`. A version offers `solo`, `multiplayer` or both. `coverFile` is an
image beside `manifest.json`, for games whose own files hold none a browser displays. The base/version overlay is the
same as for Windows games: version files replace same-named base files, whatever their case. Optional fields:

- `requires` (on the version, without `mount`): other ports' versions whose files lie beneath this version's own, in
  order — a game over another's files, as the two Counter-Strike games below over `counter-strike`'s, without a copy.
  In the page's tree, the files served and the dedicated server's linked tree alike (`gameLayers`, game-files.js).
- `goldsrc.extras`: the release's archives mounted in the game folder (`engine/valve/extras.pk3` by default, the page
  only); declared, the dedicated server gets them too (linked into its game folder). The page fetches each whole
  before the engine starts (the engine reads every member's header at the mount): only the engine's own archive belongs
  there. The files Orthros builds for a game are the release's `gamefiles/` instead ("The release's own game files",
  below), never named here.
- `goldsrc.solo.commands` / `goldsrc.multiplayer.commands`: console commands before the map, one per entry (the page;
  `+command` arguments of the dedicated server) — `maxplayers 10` and `deathmatch 1` make a solo game a listen server
  with Counter-Strike's round rules and bots (with one player the game installs its training rules: no team, no bot).
- `multiplayer.gameLibrary`: a native game library in the `engine` release that the dedicated server loads instead of
  the one the game's `liblist.gam` names (`-dll`): the server side of modules built from source.

The page starts the engine with `-dll` set to the name the engine's wrapper preloads the server module under
(`DEFAULT_SERVER_LIBRARY` of its `constants.js`): the engine otherwise opens the library the game's `liblist.gam` names
(`dlls/cs_emscripten_wasm32.wasm` for Counter-Strike), finds no such module and runs no local server — what kept
Counter-Strike at its title screen in single player, whichever server module.

## The page

`src/ports/goldsrc/play.html` has the frame of every Orthros game page (`src/host/web/shell.js`, docs/game-frame.md):
the header (game, mouse captured or free, saves, frame rate, the online games, settings, full screen, back to the
games) and the loading screen over the game's blurred cover — who plays (the Orthros account, or a warning), the
online games, the start's steps (engine, game files, the game's first images) with their progress, and tips. The game
starts at once.

- **The game's own main menu.** No mode to choose before the start: the engine starts on the game's menu, where the
  player picks single player (Half-Life's new game; Counter-Strike's multiplayer, create game) or multiplayer. The
  manifest's `solo.commands` run at the start (bots, game settings): a game the menu creates gets them; `solo.map` is
  only `check.mjs`'s. The player's name in the game is the Orthros account's (a player not signed in is `GuestNNN`,
  without multiplayer).
- **Orthros' server in the LAN games.** With `multiplayer` and a signed-in player (the server refuses the relay and
  room creation otherwise), the page opens the relay (`/api/udp/<manifest>`) as the engine starts and sends it every
  packet the engine sends, whatever its address: the menu's LAN search (a broadcast)
  reaches the version's dedicated server, whose answer comes as `127.0.0.1:8080` and lists it, with its map and players;
  joining it connects there. The server closes an idle relay after two minutes: the next packet opens a new one.

- **The game fills the window** under the header (the whole screen in full screen). SDL sizes the game's screen to the
  canvas' size on the page: the game renders at the size it is shown, without bars, whatever the window's shape, and a
  mouse position maps one to one. The page tells SDL when that size changes without the window's (the header hidden).
- **The mouse.** The engine captures it itself when the game takes it (SDL's relative mode: pointer lock at the next
  input event) and frees it in its menus and console, where its cursor shows (the canvas' CSS cursor). A click on the
  game captures it again only while the game wants it (after Esc released it in the game), never in a menu — the page
  used to lock it at every click, which left the menus without a cursor. Full screen captures it at once in the game.
  (Emscripten gives SDL positions relative to the canvas already: the page must not shift them — a version that did put
  clicks 44 pixels above the cursor, outside full screen.)
- **Large screens.** The engine's `hud_scale` (read at its start: the width of a virtual screen the HUD is drawn on) is
  set from the largest size the game takes (the screen's, full screen): none up to about 1920 × 1080, then by half steps, 1.5 at 2560 × 1440 and 2.5 at
  3840 × 2160 — the HUD, its texts and the mods' menus keep their size instead of shrinking.
- **Telemetry.** A few reports a session to `/api/telemetry` (`port: "goldsrc"`, `event`: `start`, `error` — a page
  error or an unhandled rejection —, `crash` with the end of the engine's log, `end` with the frame rate). After a crash
  the profile is saved and "Restart the game" reloads the page (an engine that stopped cannot start again in it).- **The frame rate** counts the engine's main loop iterations that drew (`postMainLoop`, draw calls seen).
- **The renderer's error checks** (`gl_check_errors`, on by default in the engine) are off unless `?debug`: the
  renderer called `glGetError` after its passes (10 a frame in Half-Life and Counter-Strike) and after each texture
  upload, and each one waits for the browser's GPU process (71-77 µs on an idle context here; on a real GPU, the CPU and
  GPU stop working in parallel). Measured (2026-10-21, `tools/goldsrc/perf.mjs --gl discard`, Half Strike de_dust2 with
  bots, walking, 20 s, three runs each, medians, machine load 18-33): the engine's work a frame 8.5 → 4.9 ms (p90 12.2
  → 7.7, p99 25.3 → 17.9), synchronous calls 10 → 0 a frame.
- **The world from buffers** (`gl_vbo 1`, off by default in the engine, "known to be glitchy" upstream; `?vbo=0` or a
  manifest's commands turn it off): without it the renderer's GLES shim sends the world a polygon at a time — its own
  buffer upload, attribute setup and vertex array switch each time, about 15 WebGL calls a draw. With it the map's
  surfaces go to buffers once at its load. Measured the same way (three runs each, medians, load 15-33): draws a frame
  718 → 86, WebGL calls 10,439 → 1,876, the engine's work a frame 4.9 → 1.7 ms (p90 7.7 → 2.7, p99 17.9 → 4.5); drawn
  by SwiftShader, the same view 19 → 55 frames a second. Checked on screenshots (SwiftShader, with and without): de_dust2,
  the same view with bullet decals — identical; Half-Life c1a0 (lightmaps, see-through grates, models; the tram's view
  turned differently) — the same rendering. Dynamic lights over the world were not compared on purpose.
  (Measured too, not changed: `getParameter` after each vertex array switch in Emscripten's glue, 70 ns; a buffer
  upload 0.6 µs either way — a rebuilt shim streaming into one buffer would win little once the world is in buffers.)
- **The menu module.** Counter-Strike's manifests name none: the engine's (`engine/libmenu.wasm`) shows the game's own
  title screens and takes the mouse; cs16-client's `mainui_cpp` (still built, `modules.builds`) wants the images of its
  `cs16client-extras` package and gets no mouse position from this engine.
- "Back to the games" writes the game's settings, saves the profile here and on the account once the player confirmed;
  the engine is not asked to quit (this release's quit can stop on a double free of its own; the page goes anyway).

## Server routes

- `/api/manifests`: every version, with `runtime`; a port also has `launchUrl` and `modes`, and is `available` only
  when its files, its engine release and the modules it names are installed. The home starts a port by opening its
  `launchUrl` (`src/host/web/main.js`); the Windows pre-download row is for `win32` versions only.
- `/ports/goldsrc/<manifest>/`, `/ports/re3/<manifest>/`: the port's page.
- `/engines/<release>/<path>`: engine files, only of releases a manifest names, cached as immutable. Pages and the
  home's Prepare are given the content addresses below instead; these keep answering for pages already open.
- `/engines/_c/<sha256>/<name>`: an engine file by its content (next section), immutable, brotli sibling as above;
  `/engines/_c/<tree sha256>/<path>`: a member of a module graph's tree; `/engines/_c/<sha256>/lean<n>/openmw.data`:
  OpenMW's lean package (docs/openmw.md).
- `/gamez/<manifest>/...?r=<start>-<end>`: the game's files, compressed when that saves bytes, as for Windows games
  (see "Streamed files" below). Native binaries (`.exe`, `.dll`, `.so`) are not part of the engine's tree.
- `/api/prefetch/<manifest>`: GET the learned list (files and pieces in the order sessions first read them); POST
  `{ session, reads: [[path, start, end, t]] }`, the reads a page served, `t` in ms since its engine started.
- `/api/udp/<manifest>` (WebSocket): the multiplayer relay. Each player gets one UDP socket to the version's dedicated
  server on `127.0.0.1:<multiplayer.port>`, never another destination; same-origin pages only, 64 players at once,
  idle connections closed after two minutes. With `?rooms` (the page's): one socket per room, each message carrying
  its room in its first byte (255: every room — the game's LAN search). A page that goes (tab closed, reload, back to
  the games) first runs the engine's `disconnect` while the relay is open, so the server drops the player at once
  (2026-10-23): before, it kept it until its timeout (a minute), and the same account back meanwhile played as
  `name (1)` beside its still body — what made the multiplayer check's last step miss player one's score.
- `/api/rooms/<manifest>`: the lobby. GET: the version's games (its permanent server and the rooms players created:
  name, map, players with the bots, humans, size, bots), the maps and the limits, from its server manager, with the
  manifest's options (without their commands) and map groups (`multiplayer.mapGroups`). POST
  `{ name, map, maxPlayers, bots }`: a room created (the page's origin; one creation in flight per address, 30 a minute in all), answered once its
  server answers, with the room's secret `key`. `DELETE /api/rooms/<manifest>/<index>` `{ key }` (the page's origin):
  that room closed — its server stopped, its players back to the menu; room 0 never. The lobby keeps the keys of the
  rooms its browser created (`localStorage`, `orthros-rooms:<manifest>`) and shows those a Close button.

### Engine files by content (2026-10-27)

Engine releases come often and change one or two files (Arsenal r2 → r12, OpenMW r1 → r11, reVC r1 → r3), and a
release-keyed URL made every file new to the browser's HTTP cache and to Prepare's. One shared mechanism,
`src/host/engine-content.js`, gives every runtime's engine files an address by their content, so that a player coming
back after a release fetches only the files whose bytes changed. The rules:

- **The sha256.** A file's address is the sha256 of its bytes as the server reads them: hashed once per file, size and
  mtime, in the background, one file at a time, its release URL given meanwhile (the installed releases' page files,
  about 500 MB, are hashed in seconds after a start). What `release.json` says — `files` as `[{ path, sha256, bytes }]`
  (Xash3D) or `{ path: sha256 }` (re3), OpenMW's `engineFiles` `{ basename: sha256 }` — is only checked against it, a
  mismatch logged: a release copied from another and then one file replaced while keeping an old mtime (`cp -p`,
  `rsync -a`, a restore) must not put its bytes, immutable for a year in browsers, under the address of the other
  release's file (or the reverse). All 727 declared sha256s of the installed releases matched their files (checked
  2026-10-27). OpenMW's lean package (openmw-lean.js) is keyed by the same hash of `openmw.data`, through the same
  `engineContent` instance (one hashing, one rule).
- **Files.** `/engines/_c/<sha256>/<name>` (`name`: the file's name in its release). The same bytes in two releases
  have one address. The route serves only a file indexed from a release a manifest names, under its own name, while
  its size and mtime are still those hashed (checked at each request: a file changed since is out of the index), with
  its release's `.br` sibling as `sendEngineFile` does. An address not indexed yet (a release installed since, or a
  server just restarted: addresses the previous process gave a page or a Prepare) indexes every manifest's engine again
  (at most every 5 s, and once after each hashing it waited for: a tree is known once all its members are hashed), and
  waits for the hashing running (up to 60 s) before it answers or 404s.
- **Module graphs are trees.** Scripts that import their siblings by relative paths (Xash3D's `engine/`: `index.js` →
  `./xash3d.js` → `./generated/xash.js`, `../utils/index.js`…) cannot each sit under their own sha256. Every script under
  the graph's directory (`GOLDSRC_MODULE_TREE`, listed or not — a module the graph imports is in it) forms one tree,
  `/engines/_c/<tree sha256>/<path in the tree>`, its sha256 made of its members' paths and sha256s: the graph keeps its
  address while no script changes, and its relative imports resolve inside it. A tree with a member not hashed yet is
  given under its release.
- **One map for the page and for Prepare.** The server's `engineUrlsOf(manifest)` (from `portEngine`: the runtime's
  files a page may load — `goldsrcPageFiles` with every language's archives, `re3EngineFiles`, `openmwEngineFiles`) is
  what `/api/manifest/<name>` gives the page as `engineUrls` `{ release path: URL }` and what `engineOf` lists for the
  home (`launch.engineFiles`, Prepare's files). The pages take an engine file's address through one helper,
  `engineUrls(config, release)` in `src/ports/port-files.js` (its content URL, else its release URL): GoldSrc's module
  import, `libraries` (the loader's `filesMap`) and extras; re3's module import and `locateFile` (its WebAssembly).
  OpenMW's page is the release's own HTML: `withEngineUrls` (openmw.js) gives `openmw.js` (its script, and the pthread
  workers it starts from its own address), `openmw.wasm` and `openmw.data` through `Module.locateFile` (the lean package
  first, `withLeanPackage`). Emscripten's own sibling URLs all go through those (`locateFile`, `filesMap`); a file
  without a content URL resolves as before.
- **Prepare.** The download worker takes any `/engines/` URL; its `only-if-cached` check finds a file kept from an
  earlier release under the same address, so a stale Prepare (its `engineFiles` no longer the card's: `launchStatus`)
  fetches again only the changed files.
- re3's `gamefiles/` (the engine's own game files) are game data, not engine files: they go through the game data
  system (`/gamez`, the OPFS store), keyed by the version's paths.

Measured (2026-10-27). For each runtime a new persistent Chromium profile booted the game once on the original release,
then the same profile booted it again on the next release. Both runs used the same code tree's server: main `a9aae1b`
for the "before" column, this change for the "after" column. Everything went through `tools/net-proxy.mjs` at 1.8 MB/s
with a 90 ms round trip, on copies of the learned state and the br-cache. Each case ran twice, with identical bytes
both times. The table gives the `/engines` bytes on the wire for the second boot:

| Release change | Before | After | Requests after |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arsenal r11 → r12 (real releases: the server and client wasm changed) | 15.05 MB (19 files) | 0.61 MB | 2 |
| reVC r3 → a copy with `revc.mjs` changed | 1.07 MB | 0.050 MB | 1 |
| OpenMW r11 → a copy with `openmw.js` changed | 5.70 MB (js + wasm) | 0.069 MB | 1 |

- **Saved per returning player:** 14.4 MB for Arsenal (about 8 s at 1.8 MB/s, about 170 s at 85 KB/s), 1.02 MB for
  reVC, and 5.63 MB for OpenMW. OpenMW's lean package was already content-addressed before this change.
- **First boot:** the same with and without the change (Arsenal 15.04 MB, reVC 1.07 MB, OpenMW 13.55 MB with its lean
  package).
- **Requests:** every engine request this change's pages made was a content URL, including OpenMW's pthread workers,
  which load from the same `openmw.js` address.
- **Browser checks:** all three passed against a server of this change: `tools/goldsrc/check.mjs half-life-original-en solo`,
  `tools/re3/check.mjs vice-city-revc --new-game` (on the changed copy) and `tools/openmw/check.mjs morrowind-goty-en`
  (on the changed copy).
- **Not measured:** Prepare's Cache Storage path, which was not exercised in a browser; real players' links.

## Streamed files

The page does not download a game before starting it: its files are the game data every Orthros game reads
(CLAUDE.md "Standardization", docs/slow-network.md) — `src/ports/port-files.js` opens it (`src/vfs/data-client.js`)
at the page's start, beside the engine's download (`openPortData`; docs/slow-network.md "Opened early"), and mounts the
version's tree in the engine's file system (`src/vfs/emscripten-files.js`: names and sizes at once, a
file's bytes at its first read). The bytes come from the data worker (`src/vfs/data-worker.js`), the Windows games'
reader in a worker of its own: the server's compressed ranges (`/gamez`), the link's measure and its regimes, the
browser's OPFS block store (`orthros-files-<manifest>`, the same the home screen's whole download fills), the learned
order fetched ahead from the game's position.

- **Startup set.** The server's learned order (`/api/prefetch`): what earlier sessions read before their game was
  playable (the page marks it where its loading screen hides, `GameData.mark('playable')`; docs/slow-network.md
  "Playable after"), else up to its first pause of 2 s — loaded before the engine starts. The home card says its size
  and time at the visitor's link, and "Prepare" downloads it ahead.
- **The rest in the background.** Once the engine runs: the learned order from the game's position, then what the
  reader's policies add (blocks around a miss, a file read in order ahead of its reader).
- **Reads not there yet.** A read of bytes not in the page waits for the worker on shared memory (the page's thread
  waits — GoldSrc), or suspends the engine (JSPI — re3; OpenMW from orthros-r19, after waiting a few ms on the page's
  thread first — 10 ms, in its loads only: `GameData.soon`, docs/openmw.md "Waits that yield to the
  browser"); the worker answers with what was asked and as much of the file as it has here already — an image (a
  texture) to its end at its first missing piece where the page asks for it (OpenMW's: `wholeLoads`; docs/slow-network.md
  "A whole image at its first missing piece").
- **Learning.** The worker reports the pieces the engine used (path, range, time since its start) to `/api/prefetch`.
- **Phases: a map's reads together.** A page whose engine has phases of its own tells them (`GameData.phase(name)`;
  GoldSrc: each map's load — an open of `maps/<map>.bsp` that reads half the file or more, `phaseOnRead` in
  `src/vfs/emscripten-files.js`; a menu listing maps reads less). The reports carry the session's phases with their
  start; the server keeps, for each block read first in a phase, its time from that phase's start, and each phase's
  usual start (the median of its sessions' starts, `phases-<manifest>.json`). The learned order then lists each phase's
  blocks together, in the order its load reads them, the phases in the order they usually come (server.js
  `prefetchList`): a session that enters a map finds that map's reads next in the list (fetched ahead from there, as
  any position in it), and the background loading goes on with the map that usually comes next — whatever the pace
  of the sessions that taught it (a player who loads a late save at once no longer puts that map's reads among the
  first map's). Blocks learned without a phase keep their time since the session's start, and so does a block some
  session read before any phase (a menu's read is not moved to a map's load). Clients' phases are bounded: 64 per
  report, 256 per version (a new one past that is not counted), 16 per learned block; a session made by a report of
  phases only is evicted like a reading one.
- **Light copies.** On a link that is not fast, a large texture's load reads its light copy first (the texture
  without its finest levels), the file itself following in the background for its next load (docs/slow-network.md
  "Light copies"; `lightCopies: false` in a version turns them off).
- **Earlier copies.** The IndexedDB copy an earlier page kept (`content`) is handed to the block store at the next
  start, then removed.
- **What the player sees.** Every game's indicators (`src/host/web/data-meter.js`, `shell.setData`): over the page,
  "Loading the game data" with the MB received, the rate, the step's percentage when the learned order tells its size —
  drawn by a worker, so it moves while the page's thread waits (GoldSrc) and shows once the engine's reads have waited
  1.5 s (re3: the page goes on painting) —; in the header, a pill while the learned order or the whole game loads in
  the background. The home screen's "download first" and the settings' offline copy (`offlineCopy`, kept in this
  browser for every game) fill the same store.

### Map loads (2026-10-22)

`tools/goldsrc/maps.mjs <manifest> --steps "wait 5,map c1a0,wait 20,changelevel c1a0d,wait 10" [--net KB/s]`: a new
browser, its page as a visitor, each step in turn (a console command, or time spent in the map); a map's load is
timed from its command to the first frame of a steady run (20 frames each within 250 ms of the one before), with the
game data's waits meanwhile (count, ms, MB), the map file's own (`bspWaits`) and the MB loaded in the background (by
producer: `bgByMB`). `--report` teaches the server (its learned order); `--report --no-phases` teaches it without the
session's phases, by time only. `--proxy <rate>:<rtt>` (e.g. `8m:85`, 2026-10-28): the page behind the player's-link
proxy (`tools/net-proxy.mjs`: HTTP/2 on one connection, as the production front) in front of `--url` instead of
Chrome's emulation (which keeps HTTP/1.1's six connections a host), its self-signed key trusted; each load's window of
the proxy's log in its line (`proxy`: the game's own requests, the ahead / announced / background bytes) and the run's
summary (`proxySummary`). `--spki <key>` / `--insecure`: an https `--url` behind a proxy started elsewhere.

Half-Life (`half-life-original-en`), Chrome's network emulation with a 40 ms round trip, a scratch server, load 25-80:

| | `map c1a0` | `changelevel c1a0d` |
|---|---|---|
| no network limit (the teacher) | 1.1-1.2 s, 434 waits (0.7 s), 25 MB | 0.8 s, 50 waits (0.3 s), 6 MB |
| 8 MB/s, the learned order of the live server (2026-10-22: no phases yet) | 3.3, 3.4 s, 435 waits (2.9-3.0 s) | 2.9, 3.0 s, 50 waits (2.0 s) |
| 8 MB/s, after one teaching session (its pace) | 0.9, 2.1 s, 432 waits (0.4-1.5 s) | 0.6, 0.55 s, 51 waits (0.1 s) |
| 8 MB/s, a slower teacher (60 s in c1a0), with phases | 0.9, 1.8 s | 0.6, 0.5 s |
| 8 MB/s, the same slower teacher, by time only | 1.8, 1.1 s | 0.6, 1.1 s |
| 1 MB/s, the live server's order | 13.9 s, 453 waits (13.4 s), 20 MB | 10.8 s, 60 waits (6.2 s), 7 MB |

At 8 MB/s a map whose reads are not ahead of the engine costs the link's round trip per wait (c1a0d: 50 waits, 2 s of
the 3); taught, its reads come before the engine asks (the background loading goes on through the map's reads during
the time in the previous map). With one teacher the phases and the time order put the same blocks first (the
difference above is the run-to-run spread); phases matter when the sessions that teach differ in pace — the live
server's order, made of sessions that wait in the menu or load a save at once, did not have c1a0's reads ahead of a
player who starts it after 5 s. At 1 MB/s c1a0 is the link's own time (20 MB to read, the background loading
beside): nothing to win there but bytes.

### Map loads announced (2026-10-27)

The engine reads its files synchronously and one at a time: each piece of a map's load that is not in the page yet is a
round trip with the page's thread held (`GameData.fetchSync`), and the learned order only fetches ahead during a load
whose position it follows (a map that no session has taught gets none of it). The map's file says much of what the load
reads next, so the page reads it (`src/ports/goldsrc/bsp-reads.js`, `announceMapLoads`, hooked on the mounted files
beside `phaseOnRead`) and announces those reads, which the data worker fetches in parallel (`GameData.want`,
`HttpBackend.wantList`). The engine's own reads join those requests.

- **When.** An open of `maps/<map>.bsp` that has read at least half the file is a load; a map listing, which reads only
  the header and the entities, is not. After the read that brings the header (BSP v30) and the entity and texture lumps
  into the page (`GameData.peek`: nothing fetched), the lumps are parsed once per open. Lumps 0 and 1 are swapped in
  some maps; the one that reads as text starting with `{` is the entities.
- **What, only what the load certainly reads:**
  - every texture the texture lump names, as the lump of the WAD the engine finds it in. The search covers the
    worldspawn's `wad` list (base names that the game has) from its end, as the engine does. Each WAD's directory is
    parsed as the engine reads it (the hook on the `.wad` nodes: at the mount, at its start, while those pieces are
    certainly in the page — a long session evicts them later); a WAD whose directory was never parsed is skipped. A
    texture whose pixels the map holds is read from the map unless the engine's `r_wadtextures` is set
    (`Mod_LoadTextureData`, mod_bmodel.c: the WAD list first then; the cvar defaults to 0 and is a game's config choice —
    Half-Life's `config.cfg` sets it, Counter-Strike's do not): announced from a WAD only then. This engine build
    answers no console query (its console output never reaches the page: `Xash3D.getCVar` times out), so the page takes
    the value the configuration the engine reads sets: the last `r_wadtextures` statement of the `.cfg` / `.rc` files as
    the engine reads them (`FS.read` watched in play.js; `configSetting`), of the language's arguments and of the
    commands the page runs; none: 0, the external textures only. (Half-Life's campaign maps embed all their textures, and with its setting their
    loads' learned reads are lumps of halflife.wad — c0a0: 98 of 104 predicted pieces among the learned ones; de_aztec
    embeds all 48 of its own, read from the map: about 1 MB that announcing them from the WADs would waste.)
  - the sky: `skyname` → `gfx/env/<name><rt|bk|lf|ft|up|dn>`, `.tga` or else `.bmp`. With no `skyname` key nothing is
    announced: the engine keeps its last sky.
  - the entities' files: a `model` key's `.mdl` / `.spr` (not a brush model `*n`), and an `ambient_generic`'s
    `message` sound under `sound/` (not a `!sentence`).
  - files beside the map: `overviews/<map>.txt` with its `.bmp` / `.tga`, when the game has them; `maps/graphs/<map>.nod`
    only when the page certainly runs the map's server (only the server's game module reads node graphs): no remote
    server joined through the relay this session (`Relay.joined`, set at the engine's connectionless `connect` through
    it — a signed-out player cannot join one).
  - the entries of `maps/<map>.res`, when there is one, of those kinds (`.wad` and `.bsp` lines aside), as a second list
    (label `res:<map>`). The engine never reads this file: at the load's announce (never at a listing) it is announced
    and fetched in the background (`GameData.ensure` — the announced request joined, so not learned as a read; read with
    `peek`, so never reported as used), and its entries announced once it is here; the page's thread never waits for it.
  - Files are looked up as the engine's search order finds them: the game's folder first, then the others it mounts,
    with a language's folder where it goes (`languageFiles`). Nothing the page already holds is announced.
- **How.** `GameData.want(entries, { label: 'textures:<map>', wait: false })`:
  - The list is posted at once (the page's thread does not yield before the engine's next reads) and carries no batch
    number, so `wantWait` never waits for it. The worker counts it in ctrl[13] and ctrl[14] only.
  - The worker passes `wait: false` on to `HttpBackend.wantList`: no `NetLink.wait` of its own (the engine's reads
    during the load make the link's silence) and the learned read-ahead not paused (`wantLoose`, not `wantLists`): the
    list holds files the load reads late too (the client's models and sounds), and on a taught map the order's next
    entries — the reads the map's file cannot predict, the game module's precaches — go meanwhile instead of a round trip
    each. It still counts as a load under way (`loadUnderWay`: the light copies' upgrades wait). On an HTTP/1.x origin
    (a local server; `NetLink.h1`) its units are 4 in flight at most (`WANT_REQUESTS_H1_LOOSE`), not 32: the browser
    runs six requests to the host at once, the others queued in their order, and 32 announced units held the engine's
    own reads and the learned read-ahead behind them — a taught map was slower with the announce (below).
  - A WAD lump is a range past the archive's start, so it is announced as what the archive's current load reads (`h.as`,
    `nextPick` with a position): the light copy on a thin link. A WAD's light copy keeps the file's size and offsets
    (`sameLayout`), so it is announced by range, not whole. The choice is pinned in case the engine opens the archive
    again.
- **Rules.**
  - Announce only what the load certainly reads: its requests are urgent and `forLoad`, so a wrong guess takes the
    link from the load's own reads.
  - No game's names, only the engine's formats and folders.
  - One WAD3 reader, shared with the server's light copies (`src/vfs/wad3.js`).
  - `?mapreads=0` turns it off to compare (`maps.mjs --query mapreads=0`).

Read-only check against the live learned order (2026-10-27, `textures:` sets of the real maps): HL c0a0 82 entries
1.9 MB, c1a0 178 / 1.9 MB, c1a0d 208 / 2.0 MB; Arsenal de_dust 38 / 3.2 MB, cs_office 124 / 3.4 MB, cs_italy 118 /
5.2 MB (all of its pieces among that map's learned reads), de_chateau 144 / 9.7 MB, cs_assault 191 / 4.7 MB, de_aztec 62
/ 5.2 MB.
