```
time left update every 5 s (~950 KB/s, "about 24 min left" for Vice City's 1.5 GB), a reload shows "1% downloaded (27 MB
of 1.5 GB) · about 24 min more" with Resume, which continues from 27 MB; Pause stops it.

```

`docs/snapshot.md`:

```md
# Snapshots of the machine

A Windows game spends 20 to 60 s reaching its menu under Orthros, 92 % of it its own start-up code: streaming the game
files faster cannot shorten that. A snapshot of the whole emulated machine taken at the menu, restored by a later
session, would let the game go on from there. Stage 1 (this document) proves it can be done exactly, in Node; stages 2
and 3 (a player's own snapshot kept in the browser, then one shared by the server) build on it.

## What a snapshot is

- **Guest memory**: every 4 KiB page holding anything (zero pages implied), the JIT's tables left out (`JIT_RANGES`:
  the restored machine translates again).
- **The emulator's JavaScript state**: everything reachable from the Vm (processes, threads, handles, heaps, windows,
  COM objects, Direct3D devices and resources, sound buffers, registry, files...), one record per object, references by
  index, typed arrays' bytes apart (`src/core/snapshot.js`).

It is taken at a **quiet point** only: between two time slices, no thread inside a dispatch loop or a callback, no nested
wait, no file read in flight; the COM calls the JIT queued are run first (`notQuiet`, `captureVm` in
`src/core/vm-snapshot.js`). A snapshot is restored in a **fresh Vm built like the captured one** (same game, files,
host, kind of clock) whose process was not created (`restoreVm`).

## Nothing left out silently

The point of the design: Orthros changes every day, and a snapshot that misses one field goes on with a machine that is
subtly wrong. So:

1. **In by default.** Every field of every reachable object is in the snapshot. A class says which of its fields are
   transient (caches, links to the host, diagnostics) and how to rebuild them (`skip`, `init`).
2. **Refused loudly.** The walk refuses what it cannot rebuild — a function, an object of a class nobody registered, an
   accessor, a view on a buffer it does not know — and names the path (`a function (hook) at
   vm.proc.threads[0].hook`). A capture that meets one fails; with a list (`captureVm(vm, meta, problems)`) it gives
   every refusal at once: the work a new kind of state needs. In production the game then starts the usual way.
3. **Known objects keep their identity.** What every Vm builds alike — the Vm itself, its memory and the memory's views,
   its API registry, its clock, its file system's mounts, the whole graph its modules leave on it once constructed
   (`SnapRegistry.knowGraph`), the containers a module keeps in its closure (`snapKnown(vm, name, container)`) — is
   referred to by name and its contents restored in place, so the closures holding it stay valid. A function in a known
   object is code: the restored Vm's own, checked to be there.
4. **Hidden state is linted.** A variable a module keeps at its top level or in a closure that takes the Vm is invisible
   to the walk. `tests/snapshot-lint.test.js` fails on every such declaration that may hold state (a `let` starting from
   a value of its own, a `const` bound to a container) unless it is handed over (`snapKnown`) or says why it is not
   state (`// snapshot: constant`, `cache`, `diagnostics`, `scratch`...). Names in capitals are constant tables by the
   sources' convention. It found, among others: process ids and window class atoms counted at the module level (shared
   by every Vm of the page), Direct3D resource and shader ids, MCI devices, GDI+ objects, kernel32's named objects and
   mutex slots.
5. **An oracle checks the result.** A machine and its restored copy, run alike, must stay the same — guest memory and
   every object of the state (`snapshotsDiffer`). `tests/snapshot.test.js` does it on the test programs (threads,
   synchronization, priorities, timers, DirectX, MCI) in `make test`; `tools/snapshot-check.mjs` on games. A field a
   change adds and the restore misses makes them differ: the DirectSound counter of logged buffers, believed to be mere
   diagnostics, was caught that way.

## Special cases

- **Parked threads.** A thread blocked in an API call at top level is parked with closures the call made (its wake
  condition, what it claims on wake-up), its call rolled back to the thunk. At a restore the call is executed again as at
  its first try to make them again, then the snapshot's state is put back over what that changed (`decodeGraph`'s
  `reimpose`) and the wait keeps its deadline. No blocking API needs code of its own, present or future.
- **API thunks.** The registry is restored by name: which DLL function each slot holds, the handlers the restored Vm's
  own. Handlers a module defines as the game reaches them (COM methods) are defined again by name (`ApiRegistry.lazyDefs`).
- **Open files** are opened again by their path, at the same position (`FileHandle`). In-memory mounts (files the game
  wrote outside its profile) are kept with their contents; the others are the host's: the game's files, and the
  player's profile — a **persistent mount** (`MemBackend.seen`), see below.
- **The host's side** of the machine's objects is not in a snapshot: what a backend keeps on a Direct3D resource (the
  WebGL backend's texture record, the recorder's mirror record — its shader and declaration ids live in its own
  `WeakMap`), the sound mixer's voice table and slots, the recorder's marks on state tables. A restored resource is one
  no backend has seen: created and uploaded whole at its first use. What the host showed comes back through `resume`
  hooks (`snapshotClass(cls, { resume })`, run once the machine is whole): the window manager sets the display mode,
  title and cursor again.
- **Several processes** (a game started by its launcher, docs/processes.md): a machine that started a child process is
  never captured (`notQuiet`: "several processes") — its state spans several machines, each with its own memory.
- **CPU states** are views on the guest memory (rebuilt by address); a PE image's file bytes, only read while it was
  mapped, are not kept.
- **Time** goes on from where it was: a virtual clock's state, a real clock's origin moved. Everything the guest can
  observe reads the guest's clock, never the host's: the time stamp counter (RDTSC: it read `performance.now()`, which
  made BFME2's copy compute other values from the same state), kernel32's Sleep(0) storms — the same on a real clock,
  continuous across a snapshot, deterministic on a virtual one.
- **The JIT** starts empty in the restored machine. `Vm.resetJit()` gives the original an empty one too, so both
  translate alike: the oracle then compares them at the JIT's speed.

## Results (stage 1, Node, virtual clock)

`node tools/snapshot-check.mjs <manifest> --games-dir /srv/orthros/data/games [--at <s> | --input <scenario> --at-mark
<label>] [--jit] [--input-after <scenario>] [--then <slices>] [--every <slices>]`

| game, capture | objects | guest memory | snapshot (raw) | restore | then |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vice City, menu (130 s) | 3 792 | 25 MiB (6 395 pages) | 28.5 MiB | 0.09 s | a new game started, the city loaded, driven: identical for 200 000 slices (87 s of game, 7.5 M API calls) |
| BFME2 1.09, 120 s (first-launch benchmark) | 35 368 | 112 MiB (28 575 pages) | 119.6 MiB | 0.37 s | identical for 3 000 slices |
| BFME2 1.09, 180 s (drawing, 8 threads) | 35 609 | 119 MiB (30 498 pages) | 127.2 MiB | 0.4-0.8 s | identical for 120 000 slices (30 s of game) |

Compressed sizes (study of 2026-10-14): Vice City ~15 MB, BFME2 ~39 MB at zstd -19. Under Node with an empty profile
BFME2 spends its first 130 s of game time in its first-launch benchmark; its 3D menu was not reached there with the
harness's startup scenario (18 draws per frame where the scenario waits for 150): the skirmish comparison is still to do.

## In the page: a player's own snapshot (stages 1b and 2)

A session takes one **once the game settled**: no file opened for 4 s while it went on presenting frames (a loading
step over), at the next quiet point (`src/host/snapshot-watch.js`, the worker's `snapshotAutoStep`) — then again at each
later settled stretch after more files were opened, until the player's first click or key: an intro that streams its
video from a file already open settles too, the menu after it is a later point. A session restored from a snapshot goes
on the same way. A capture refused — a movie playing, a kind of state not supported yet — is tried again after the next
settled stretch, four times at most. The page keeps it in OPFS
(`orthros-snapshot-<manifest>/machine.bin`, then `machine.json` with its key, written last; the data manager counts it
with the game's cache and clears it with it) once the session went on for 20 s more **with the profile still as the
snapshot's machine saw it** — the next start would refuse it otherwise: a game often writes its settings as it reaches
its menu, just after a screen where it settled first; that snapshot is dropped and another taken at the next settled
stretch. The capture stalls the game once, for 0.6 s in Vice City (most of it reading the 2 GB of guest memory for its
pages: a WebAssembly SIMD scan, bounded by the page faults of the untouched pages). The next start of the game goes on
from it when:

1. **its key is the same** (the page): Orthros' **state-owning sources** — the modules the emulator worker loads,
   followed from `src/core/vm.js` and `src/host/web/worker.js` through their imports, but for the JIT's translator and
   the GPU backends, which a restore rebuilds anyway, and the game data's transport (`/api/snapshot-sources`,
   `src/host/snapshot-sources.js`: a deployed change to the JIT or the WebGL backend keeps snapshots, one to an API
   module or the machine does not; `tests/snapshot-lint.test.js` fails if a module left out registers snapshot state).
   **Rules for the data modules** (since 2026-10-28, `DATA_TRANSPORT`): how the game's bytes come and when —
   `src/vfs/game-data.js`, `http-backend.js`, `net-link.js`, `opfs-store.js`, `launch-set.js`, `playable-watch.js`
   (and what only they import, `pcm-codec.js`) — and when a snapshot is taken (`src/host/snapshot-watch.js`) are out:
   the mounts are host objects (`state: false`, `src/core/vm-snapshot.js`), a file is reopened by its path. Which files
   the guest sees and their sizes stay in through the version's tree itself; `src/vfs/game-tree.js` (`KEPT`) holds only
   the tree's helpers. How the guest's stat/readdir/open are answered from the tree (`HttpBackend.lookup/stat/readdir`:
   case folding, directories listed before files, a directory's date 0) is out with `http-backend.js` and pinned by a
   test instead (`tests/snapshot-lint.test.js`): a change that alters what the guest reads (a size, a listing, a byte)
   fails it and belongs in a kept module or must change the tree; one that does not is restored over — a failed restore
   falls back to a cold start. Which part serves a file (`game-data.js`'s `partOf`) is out too: the owner holds the same
   bytes. Before: 48 of the 246 key changes of October were data-only commits (all 4 of 10-27's), each a cold
   start of 35-50 s to the menu for a returning BFME1 player instead of a ~0.6 s restore. A comment-only edit of
   `http-backend.js` or `game-data.js` now keeps the hash (`c707f1…` → `823bb2…` before, unchanged after); one of
   `game-tree.js` still changes it. Over October's commits, 272 → 226 change the key. Measured again 2026-10-28
   (`snapshotSourcesHash` on copies of the main tree and this one, a comment appended): main 106 modules, `cfc369…` →
   `25a966…` after `http-backend.js` + `game-data.js`; now 98 modules, `27706d…` → `27706d…` (kept), → `2918d5…` after
   `game-tree.js`. Not measured: a browser restore across a data-module edit (`tools/snapshot-browser-check.mjs`), and
   the live gain — no Win32 session in the telemetry since 10-23. — The game version's manifest and
   file tree (sizes, dates), the language and the options that change the machine (`?timescale`, `?interp`, `?dbg`...;
   `src/host/web/snapshot-key.js`). The debug flags that only measure the host's GL side are not among them
   (`HOST_ONLY_DBG` in `src/gfx/gpu-probe.js`: `ORTHROS_GL_COUNT`, `ORTHROS_GL_PROBES`, `ORTHROS_GL_TIME`; a flag joins
   the list only if it changes neither what the guest sees nor when): a `?bench` page adds `ORTHROS_GL_COUNT`, and until
   2026-10-27 that alone gave it a key of its own — the shared-snapshot jobs its 404s queued could never be published
   (the publishing session is a plain page: "this session's key is X, the server was asked for Y"), which is why no
   BFME1 1.08 or BFME II shared snapshot existed. The bench/plain key equality is covered by
   `tests/snapshot-key.test.js` only (a bench page and a plain page get the same key; no browser run checked a `?bench`
   page against a plain publisher). Separately, `tools/snapshot-shared-check.mjs bfme1-108 --lang fr --queue` on a
   private server (2026-10-27; plain pages only, which shared their key before as well) proves the BFME1 1.08
   publish/restore chain: published at 252 s of its session (310.6 MiB, 93 MB brotli), a second new player restored it
   in 623 ms — PASSED;
2. **its machine's start is this session's** (the worker, before anything changes: `snapshotStale`): the registry the
   process starts with (seeded from the manifest, the player's settings), and every path of the player's profile (as
   the manifest's `profileMoves` left it, docs/startup.md: moved before anything is recorded) the game had seen — its existence and size (`stat`), its listing (`readdir`), its bytes (`open`) — is as it saw it. The
   profile is never the snapshot's: it stays the player's, kept by the browser; saves made after the snapshot in a
   folder the game had not listed leave it valid, a changed setting or a new save where the game had listed its saves
   gives a usual start (and a new snapshot, the old one deleted).

A restore that fails midway (not refused beforehand) leaves a machine in pieces: the page deletes the snapshot and
starts again. `?snapshot=0`: none (a bench that measures a cold start passes it; `?benchsuite=...&snapshot=0` passes it on to
every game); headless runs: none unless `?snapshot=auto`. A headed `?bench` page restores like a returning player — its
own snapshot, else the server's shared one, under the players' key since 2026-10-27 — and its record says which
(`snapshot`: `own`, `shared`, `failed` or null). `window.orthros.snapshot()` takes one
now, `saveSnapshot()` keeps it as the automatic one.

`tools/with-browser-slot.sh node tools/snapshot-browser-check.mjs <manifest> --games-dir /srv/orthros/data/games`: a
session with automatic snapshots until it kept one, then the page opened again (`--manual --at <s>`: asked for at that
time).

| game | snapshot | taken in (graph, pages, encoding) | restored in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vice City, menu | 28.5 MiB | 0.6 s (20, 580, 36 ms) — 3.2 s with the earlier JavaScript page scan | 67-90 ms |

## Shared by the server (stage 3)

A player with no profile of a game yet (a first launch in this browser) and no snapshot of its key asks the server
for its **shared snapshot** (`/api/snapshot/<manifest>?key=&lang=`, `src/host/snapshot-store.js`): the one a new
player's session took on the server itself. When there is none, the server (`--snapshot-jobs`) opens the game in a
headless browser as a new player would — the same page and worker, the shared first-launch profile — with
`?snapshot=publish`: each snapshot that session keeps is posted back with the job's token, the later ones replacing the
first, until its loading is over (`tools/snapshot-publish.mjs`, one session at a time, through the browser slot
guard). Made in a browser rather than in Node: the machine sees the same host as a player's (text measured by the
browser's fonts, the audio worklet, the display). It carries the profile as its game had it at the capture (the folders
and settings it wrote while starting): a new player's profile — nothing of their own, at most the shared first-launch
files the session started from too — is made so before the worker's checks, which then pass as for a player's own
snapshot; nothing of a player is ever replaced. Another first-launch profile learned since makes it stale (the server
then makes a new one). Kept with the learned data (`<learn>/snapshots/`), gzip- and
brotli-compressed, the two most recent keys per game version and language. Not downloaded when it would take longer
than 60 s at the connection's last measured rate; kept as the player's own once it applied.

The page keeps a snapshot by writing it to OPFS in 16 MiB pieces, and the publishing session posts it once kept, from
the stored file (a disk-backed body). Until 2026-10-21 the whole buffer went to one OPFS write and, at the same time,
to the POST as a body of the bytes: copies of a few hundred MiB beside the 2 GB guest, and the publishing sessions of
the BFME games ended in "Target crashed" (RotWK 2.01 / 2.02 on the live server, 129 and 200 s, each after one
248 MB snapshot had reached the server). Measured on BFME1 1.08
fr (seeded first launch, 303.7 MiB snapshot, renderer RSS sampled every 2 s, one run each): before, the RSS climbed
from 2.0 to 4.39 GB after the keep and the page crashed at 127 s before the store finished; after, 2.47 GB at most,
kept at 73 s, published at 99 s (318 MB raw, 107 MB gzip, 94 MB brotli), and a new player's session restored it in
610 ms. `tools/snapshot-publish.mjs` prints the session's snapshot lines as they come (a session that ends badly has
said how far it got) and waits for a post in flight.

A sandboxed server (the production service: a dynamic user, no home, its own /tmp) does not start browsers: with
`--snapshot-queue` it only queues the request with its token (`<learn>/snapshots/queue.json`), and
`tools/snapshot-jobs.mjs --queue <file> --server <url>`, run outside the sandbox (the `orthros-snapshot-jobs` service),
runs the sessions through the browser slot guard. `node tools/snapshot-shared-check.mjs <manifest> [--queue]`: the whole
path on a private server — a first new player, the server's session, a second new player who must start from it.

```

`docs/startup.md`:

```md
# Start-up and first use

What Orthros does so that a game reaches its menu sooner and does not stall the first time it uses something. All
of it is generic (nothing names a game) and each part can be switched off.

## Shared first-launch profile (`src/host/profile-seed.js`)

Some games do a long piece of work on their very first launch only — while no settings file exists in the user
profile they measure the machine, build caches, choose detail levels — and skip it at every later launch (BFME2 and
RotWK: ~70 s of computation before the first frame under Orthros). A player's browser starts with an empty emulated
profile (`C:\Users\Player`), so every new player paid it.

- **Learning.** A session whose profile was empty at start watches it. At the first click that finds files in the
  profile (the game reached a screen the player acts on, its first-launch work written), or at the first character
  typed (whatever is there then), it takes a snapshot of the profile's small files: not under `Temp`, ≤ 64 KiB each,
  ≤ 128 KiB and 32 files in all (saves, previews and caches stay out). The snapshot is taken as the input arrives,
  before the game sees it: nothing the player types is in it. Once the session has gone on (600 more frames over at
  least a minute: not a launch that failed), it is posted to `POST /api/profile-seed/<manifest>` with the game
  language and the session id.
- **Consensus.** The server keeps, per manifest and game language, the distinct sets reported (identified by
  content) with the sessions that reported each. A set is offered only once `--profile-seed-quorum` distinct reporters
  (default 2) reported it identical — the most reported one wins. A reporter is a client address (behind the reverse
  proxy the first `X-Forwarded-For` hop, kept hashed): one client cannot make up the quorum with invented session
  ids; on a loopback connection without a proxy header (harness, local server) it is the session id. Identical files from independent sessions are the
  game's defaults, not one player's data. Bounded: 16 sets per manifest (least recently reported out), 32 session
  ids per set. Stored in `<learn dir>/profileseed-<manifest>.json`; a server without this feature ignores the file,
  and the page asks for it only when `/api/config` says `profileSeed: true` (old pages and servers keep working).
- **Canonical sets** (`tools/profile-seed-make.mjs`, `<learn dir>/seedcanon-<manifest>.json`). What a first-launch
  benchmark writes depends on the emulated machine's speed (the load of the machine running it, the instrumentation:
  two runs wrote `AudioLOD = High` and `Low`), so independent players rarely report identical sets and the quorum
  rarely forms (live data, 2026-10-21: one reporter per set after weeks, nothing served). An operator therefore makes,
  per version and game language, one set the server offers first, with no reporter and whatever sessions report since
  (a report only adds a candidate to the learned sets). The tool iterates the catalog (no game named): `plan` lists every
  Win32 version × declared language and what the learn directory holds; `make` runs `--runs` first launches with an
  empty profile through the browser slot guard (`headless.mjs --profile-seed 0 --profile-dir`), compares their seed
  files and writes them when they agree (`--accept first`: the first run's); `put` takes a profile directory (a run's,
  possibly edited by hand: the settings it carries become every new player's default), `promote` a learned set,
  `show` / `remove`. The server reads the file again when it changes (no restart). The snapshot key's seed part is
  the served set's key: shared snapshots made with another seed are made again.
- **Use.** A session whose profile is empty (first launch in this browser) asks
  `GET /api/profile-seed/<manifest>?lang=<game language>` (3 s at most) and writes the files before the game starts;
  they are then saved to OPFS like the game's own. It does not learn (only unseeded first launches teach).
- **Off:** manifest compat flag `"profileSeed": false` (nothing offered nor learned for that game), `?profileseed=0`
  (page), `--profile-seed 0` (harness).

The files are the game's own output under Orthros (e.g. its options file with the detail level its first-launch
benchmark chose on the emulated machine); a player can change them in the game's options as usual.

## Profile moves (`src/vfs/profile-moves.js`, manifest `profileMoves`)

A manifest change can move where a game keeps its files in the player's profile — typically a registry value its
installer writes, added to the manifest later (BFME1's `UserDataLeafName`: without it the game wrote `Options.ini`,
saves and replays straight into `AppData\Roaming`; with it, into `AppData\Roaming\My Battle for Middle-earth Files`,
as on Windows). Players who played before would lose their settings and saves. The manifest then declares
`"profileMoves": [{ "from": "AppData/Roaming", "to": "AppData/Roaming/My Battle for Middle-earth Files" }]`
(optionally `names`: only those entries of `from`):

- **When.** At every start, once the profile is assembled and before the game sees it: the page's worker after the
  browser's copy (OPFS) — into which the account's copy was restored before (`cloud-sync.js` `pull`) — the harness's
  `--profile-dir` files and a shared first-launch profile (a set learned before the change is moved like the rest);
  the Node runner (`src/host/cli.js`) on its save folder. Every entry of `from` but the folder holding `to` goes to
  `to/<name>`, folders merged.
- **Never destructive.** A file whose new place already holds one stays at the old place (the new place's is the
  game's own, newer). **Idempotent** without a marker: once moved there is nothing left to move; a later start does
  nothing (the profile the game sees is its files alone).
- **Kept everywhere.** The moves are recorded as changes of the profile (`MemBackend.changes`; `rmdir` added for the
  emptied folders, keeping their original-case name): the browser's copy follows at the first flush
  (`src/vfs/profile-opfs.js`: the files written at their new place first, then removed from the old one — only once
  every write succeeded, what failed kept for the next flush, so a closed tab or a failed write never leaves a save in
  neither place —, folders removed after their files), the worker then says `profile-changed` and the page sends
  the moved profile to the account (a push from the parent it restored: no conflict). Another device restoring an
  older copy moves it the same way.
- **Snapshots.** A snapshot key includes the manifest (the registry seeded from it): the change that needs a move
  makes every snapshot of the version stale (player's and shared: made again). The moves run before the profile's
  `seen` record starts, so a snapshot taken afterwards checks the new layout.
- **What the server keeps.** Shared first-launch sets (`profileseed-*.json`, `seedcanon-*.json`) made before the
  change still carry the old paths: harmless (moved at the client), but the canonical ones should be made again with
  `tools/profile-seed-make.mjs` so new players' profiles, and the snapshot key's seed part, match the new layout.

## Translated code kept across sessions (`src/cpu/jit/code-cache.js`)

The regions earlier sessions translated (the server's learned list, D056) are translated again at every launch by
the background translator (D058): ~27 000 regions, ~10 s of a core at each BFME2 start (~1.2 s of it compiling).
The background translator now keeps its translations in an OPFS file per game (`orthros-jitcache/<manifest>.bin`)
and reuses them at later launches:

- An entry is one region's WebAssembly body with what it was a function of. Before reuse the background worker runs
  the discovery pass on the code in memory now and requires the same entry and x87 mode asked, the same extent
  (blocks), the same code bytes there (compared byte for byte) and the same import slots holding the same fast-API
  thunks for the calls it runs inline. Its table index is the only other input: the body's one reference to it (the
  load of its next x87-mode version's slot, always a 5-byte LEB) is rewritten (`patchAltSlot`). The emulator's
  install then checks the bytes against memory as for any background translation.
- Code heat (`docs/jit-code-shape.md`: regions cut at cold exits, visit flags) is a translation input that varies by
  session and grows during one. It reaches a translation through two things only: the extent discovery finds (the
  cold edges cut — compared like any extent) and the blocks given a visit flag (those the heat does not know to have
  run). An entry is reused when it flags every block of it the heat of now does not know (`missHeat` otherwise);
  a block it flags that the heat learned since has its flag store sent to a byte never harvested (a "sink"), so
  the session reports the same blocks as a fresh translation would. (Until 2026-10-04 every heat answer the
  translation got was recorded and compared — branch sources included, which only matter through the extent: most
  "other heat" misses were entries that served.) Its visit flags are moved to the session's own flag bytes
  (`patchVisitSlots`, like the table index); a translation made when the flag area ran out is not kept. Batches
  translated under in-session options (`Jit.switchOpts`) are neither looked up nor kept. The learned entries skipped
  as blocks of an earlier region are those of the regions as cut by the heat of now: an entry a cut region no longer
  holds is translated on its own (a server that forgot it as covered relearns it at its next miss).
- One shape per code: the learned heat only grows, so an entry whose code is in memory now (its own extent compared
  byte for byte) but whose shape the heat of now no longer gives (another extent, or a block it leaves unflagged that
  the heat does not know) would not serve again — the translation added for that region supersedes it (its record
  marked unused in place). Other code at the same address (another program loaded there) keeps up to 4 variants.
- Shapes brought up to the heat of the session's end (`bg-translate.js` refresh). The heat grows during a session
  (visit flags harvested every 10 s): a region translated at the session's start would get another extent at the
  next launch, under the heat this session taught, and be translated again while that launch starts. Once the heat
  grew and no batch came for a second (the learned regions in place), the background worker discovers again the
  regions it answered in the session — only those whose blocks or branch successors gained heat since — and keeps a
  translation of those whose shape changed (not installed; it supersedes the earlier shape): the next launch finds
  the shape its heat gives. Passes in 10 ms slices with as long a pause after each (half a core at most; batches
  answered between them), again each time the heat grew, 20 s apart at the soonest; their translations' visit flags
  point at the sink byte (relocated at reuse).
- Measured with heat (2026-10-04, `integ-1004`, phase scenarios, one persistent browser profile and learn directory
  per game reused across runs): RotWK 2.02 run 1 (no heat yet) 12 991 entries added; run 2 (heat of run 1: 24 887
  ranges) 2 665 reused, 5 830 other extent, 3 609 other heat, the cache full and stale, emptied and refilled; run 3
  (heat 27 122 ranges) 8 122 reused, 312 other extent, 240 other heat (the rest new entries). BFME2 run 2 (heat
  24 887 ranges): 1 714 reused, 5 299 other extent, 2 413 other heat, emptied as well — a first BFME2 session alone
  writes 198 MiB of the 256 MiB, so the second one fills it (review re-run: 1 713 reused, 5 272 other extent, 2 404
  other heat, same rendering in play). While the learned heat still grows the cache mostly missed; it served again
  once the heat settled. See "Translated code cache over a game's first sessions" below for the build that followed (B there).
- The cache key is a hash of the translator's own sources — the import closure of `bg-translate.js`, `jit.js` and
  `runtime.js`, fetched by the worker like the modules themselves — plus the translation options and the defaults they complete (`JIT_DEFAULTS`: layout, cold exits, region sizes...): any change to the
  translator or its options empties the cache. Instrumented translations (profiling, block counters) are not kept.
- Records appended (~7 KiB per region, 70 % of it WebAssembly: 30 000 BFME2 regions take ~205 MiB), a cut tail
  dropped at load; each record starts with a binary index (entry, x87 mode, extent, inline-API slots) — the only part
  read at load; its meta JSON is parsed at a hit — and holds the number of the last session that added or reused
  it. 256 MiB per game: an addition past it (up to 9/8 of it) asks for room at the next idle moment of the background
  worker (3 s without a batch: the learned regions in place), so that no batch waits for it; past 9/8 the room is made
  at once. Making room: the entries of earlier sessions no session used for longest are evicted down to 3/4 of the
  bound (never this session's: a session whose own entries fill the file stops adding), then the file is compacted in
  place (the live records moved over the unused ones, in file order; the header says a compaction is under way until
  it is done — one cut short, the tab closed, starts the cache over at the next load). A game update (other code at
  the same addresses) is handled the same way: its old entries stop being used and are evicted first. Only the index
  stays in memory, a record is read back on a hit; one tab at a time (the OPFS file is opened for exclusive
  synchronous access: another tab runs without it).
- **Off:** `?codecache=0`; harness runs use it only with a persistent browser profile (`--opfs`), `--code-cache 0`.

## What a phase will use, prepared ahead (learned lists, D056/D058)

The server learns per manifest, in the order sessions first needed them (time since the page started, the earliest
over sessions — so menu, then map load, then play), the game file blocks read (`/api/prefetch`), the GL programs
built at a draw (`/api/programs`) and the entries of the regions translated at a miss (`/api/regions`). A new session
downloads the blocks in the background while the network is idle (the game's own reads first), compiles the programs
a few per frame without waiting for them, and has the background worker translate the regions on another core: what
a later phase needs is ready when that phase comes, without taking the game's thread. A game's dependencies (a game
mounted beside it, e.g. an expansion's base game) have lists of their own, learned from the reads of every game
mounting them.

- **Learned GL programs and translator changes** (`program-id.js`). The programs are Orthros' own GLSL: a change of
  the translators makes the learned sources useless. A fixed-function program over an FVF layout (`ff:f<fvf>:…|ff:…`
  keys, BFME1's 127 of 134) is built from its key alone (`ffProgramFromKey`, the draw path too), so a session rebuilds
  learned ones with its own translator. Every other entry carries the `PROGRAM_GLSL_VERSION` of the session that built
  or took it; a session asks `/api/programs/<manifest>?v=<its version>` and gets only those of its version (plus,
  for a few sessions, entries from before versions existed). `tests/program-version.test.js` hashes the GLSL of a
  fixed corpus: a translator change that alters it fails until the version is raised. Measured (framebench
  `--programs`, BFME1 menu, the live list of Oct 1): programs built at a draw 51 → 8, learned ones taken 1 → 44.

- **Learned entries that are blocks of an earlier learned region** (`bg-translate.js`, `Jit.bgInstallNow`). The JIT
  enters a region at any of its blocks (block hash), so a learned entry that is a block of a region installed before
  it was always dropped at install — after being translated (and, with the cache, stored). Sessions that reach code
  at different points learn such entries in numbers: 45 % of RotWK's and 42 % of Vice City's learned lists. The
  background worker now skips an entry that is a block of a region it translated before in the session (no
  translation, nothing cached); an entry whose covering region the emulator did not install (its code changed, or it
  was translated on the game thread first) is asked again once; and the worker reports the skipped entries to the
  server, which forgets them (`covered` in the POST; older servers ignore it, the file format is unchanged): their
  room in the 40 000 entries served goes to regions of later phases.

- **Borrowed entries** (`server.js` borrowedFor, 2026-10-23). A version's order holds only what its own sessions
  read: a phase none of them reached yet (a first map load after a new release, or after its order was pruned) is read
  on demand, one parked read after another. /api/prefetch now appends to the version's own order what the other
  versions' sessions read of the files it shares with them — the same file on disk (device, inode, size, time) under the
  same path: a game's versions over one base, the version another game mounts (RotWK's BFME II 1.06) —, in their own
  order, each file block once (the version's own entry first), flag 0: never in the launch set, after every entry of
  its own (at most 4096, the order's 8192 in all), so it comes with the network idle in the menus. Only a version
  some session marked playable borrows (the flags keep the borrowed entries out of its launch set). Made again a
  minute later at most; `--no-learn-borrow` turns it off. What it adds to a first launch with the live orders of
  2026-10-23: RotWK 2.02 +21 MiB of pieces for its own files (from 2.01) and +159 MiB for BFME II 1.06's (from 1.09),
  BFME II 1.09 +79 MiB (from 1.06), BFME 1.08 +225 MiB (from 1.03 and the original release).

### Why RotWK 2.02 and BFME II waited for data in the bench suite of 2026-10-23 (measured the same day)

The live baseline's first launches (`--suite all`, fresh browser) waited 1.5 / 4.3 / 1.7 s for game data in RotWK's
load, loading screen and play, BFME II 0.8 / 2.9 s in its load and loading screen. Every read that waited was missing
from the learned order (`?netlog=1`: learned rank `-` for all of them): no session of either version had loaded a map
with its order as it was. BFME II's map load had been learned in its mask-less entries, which the prune of 2026-10-21
(`tools/learn-prune.mjs --write`) dropped (its backup holds 225 of the 230 blocks the menu-only run below waited for;
the tool now drops a mask-less entry only when proven stale, docs/slow-network.md "Mask-less learned orders");
RotWK 2.02's order (and BFME II 1.06's, which RotWK mounts) had only been taken to the menu (the snapshot jobs' and
launch sessions). The baseline session itself taught them: a fresh browser on a copy of the live learn directory of
the same morning (the baseline and one more session learned) waited 0 / 17 / 31 ms (RotWK) and 14 / 73 / 230 ms
(BFME II) in those phases; the learned orders then hold 97 % of the blocks the menu-only runs waited for. Map-load
reads repeat from one session to the next (the same map); what does not is reads of play (sounds, textures of what
comes into view: rank `-` in every run). Measured with the orders cut to their launch set (the state of the baseline)
— `tools/bench-suite-check.mjs --suite <bench> --gl-discard --query netlog=1 --log <file>`, a server of this tree on a
copy of the live learn directory and br-cache, two runs side by side on the shared server (load 17-31):

|---|---|---|---|

(RotWK: its own order and BFME II 1.06's cut, BFME II 1.09's whole; BFME II: its order cut, 1.06's whole.) Other

## Game file reads on the network: short slices, block store index log (2026-10-06)

**Short slices while a read is in flight** (`src/host/web/worker.js` pump, `Vm.runFor`). A ReadFile of data still on
the network parks its thread while the others run; the fetch then needs several event-loop tasks of the worker (the
response, its body, the promise chain), and each waited behind a 12 ms pump slice of the other threads. While
`vm.readsInFlight > 0` the pump now asks for 2 ms slices, and `runFor` ends a slice once a read went in flight during
it and 2 ms have passed (`vm.readSliceMs`; `?dbg=ORTHROS_READ_SLICE_MS=12` restores the earlier behaviour, also
switchable within a session). This was the "~55 ms per read on the client side" left open above.

**Block store index log** (`src/vfs/opfs-store.js`). The JSON index was rewritten whole and synced, with the data
file, every 16 blocks: 55-59 times over a BFME2 first launch, 2.5-2.9 s of the game thread. The index is now an
append-only binary log (`index.bin`, format 3: fixed fields + key + record checksum), appended and flushed every 2 s
or 256 blocks and when forced (prefetch end, stop); a v2 `index.json` is read once and rewritten as a log. Most of the
old cost was the data file's flush (write-back of every block since the last one, ~4 ms per MiB at any
cadence): the data file is now flushed only at close — a block a crash lost fails its checksum at read and is fetched
again, as a damaged one already was.

Measured A = `main` (cab0b4c), B = this build, concurrent pairs on the shared server (other sessions' browsers
running), order alternated, fresh copy of the live learn dir per run, `--games-dir`, no block store (fresh browser):
RotWK 2.02 with `rotwk-startup.txt` and the `rotwk-202` profile, `--net-log`. "Parked" = fetch time of the reads that
parked their thread (`[net]` lines, ~570 per run); "ioWait" = the `ioWait` category of the load and loadscreen phases;
"match drawn" = the first second after the loadscreen mark whose frames carry > 150 draws (the loading screen draws
60-110). The scenario's `waitfps:12` (play mark) is unusable on this loaded server: the match runs at 9-14 fps in
both builds, so the play mark came 20-170 s after the match in either build at random.

| pair (first) | parked p50 / p90 ms | ioWait s | first frame s | menu s | load click → match drawn s | page start → match drawn s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (A) | 56 / 66 → 14 / 27 | 11.9 → 3.1 | 32 → 29 | 57 → 54 | 27 → 19 | 114 → 105 |
| 2 (B) | 56 / 66 → 15 / 27 | 11.8 → 3.1 | 31 → 27 | 57 → 51 | 26 → 28 | 114 → 107 |
| 3 (A) | 56 / 66 → 15 / 29 | 12.1 → 3.5 | 31 → 28 | 57 → 52 | 30 → 28 | 117 → 109 |
| 4 (B) | 56 / 65 → 14 / 27 | 11.9 → 3.3 | 31 → 28 | 57 → 52 | 28 → 23 | 115 → 102 |
| `--net 40:100` (A) | 84 / 116 → 59 / 93 | 23.3 → 17.4 | 41 → 40 | 66 → 66 | 34 → 33 | 131 → 129 |

- The parked reads are 4 times faster and the idle time waiting for them drops by 8.5 s per run, but most of the gain
  is before the map: the first frame comes 3-4 s and the menu 5-6 s earlier (the start-up's own parked reads). The map
  load itself (click → match drawn) gains −8, +2, −2, −5 s (and −1 s at 40 ms RTT): after an earlier menu the click
  comes while more of the background work (code translated ahead, prefetch) is still pending. From page start to the
  drawn match: 7-13 s earlier in every pair, 2 s at 40 ms RTT (where the round trip itself dominates the read).
- Vice City (`vicecity-drive.txt`, 4 pairs, 2 with `--net-log`): frames > 40 ms per minute in the drive 100 → 109,
  187 → 218, 79 → 81, 128 → 78 (A → B; mean 124 → 122), 29.8-29.9 fps and 0.2 ms host per frame in both builds; 1-3
  network reads during the drive (~1 470 parked reads per run, p50 5-6 ms in both builds: answered within a slice).

Block store, BFME2 first launch, `--opfs` (fresh browser profiles), 50 s, 2 pairs (A first, B first), then a second
launch on each profile (40 s):

| pair | store writes ms (index syncs, of which ms) A | B | second launch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 (A first) | 3 482 (55, 2 477) | 1 141 (15, 59) | 818 / 818 blocks read back, no store emptied |
| 4 (B first) | 3 573 (59, 2 928) | 1 260 (15, 122) | 818 / 813 blocks read back, no store emptied |

An intermediate build that kept the data file's flush at each sync point: 3 218 and 3 287 ms (15 syncs, 2 153-2 167 ms)
against 3 558 and 3 846 ms for A — the syncs' cost was the data file's write-back, not the JSON. The remaining ~1.2 s is
the 1 MiB block writes themselves. No Direct3D frame came within the 50 s of a BFME2 first launch in any run (its
first-launch work), so first-frame and `late` times were not comparable there.

## Canonical first-launch profile, measured (2026-10-21)

BFME1 1.08 fr, headless Chromium (SwiftShader, `--gl-discard --memprefetch`), a fresh copy per run of the live learned

  of worker time over 20 s for added state). What would remove the 2.2 % is a cheaper message (fewer, larger batches
```
